* **`Run` is idempotent**, keyed on the task version. A run record on the sandbox’s disk (`/gritz/run.json`) lets a restarted driver answer for a run it can no longer see.
* **There is no shim.** The AWS hook surface stays, but only as acknowledgements served by the driver on Lambda.

### Service definition

[Section titled “Service definition”](#service-definition)

New module `proto/driver/v1/driver.proto`, generated into `internal/proto/driver/v1` by the existing `buf.gen.yaml` (protocolbuffers/go + connectrpc/go). It imports the `gritz.v1` messages it carries (`Task`, `Event`, `TaskLink`, `RunnerEvent`) but is otherwise separate from `gritz.proto`, so it evolves on its own cadence.

```protobuf
syntax = "proto3";


package driver.v1;


import "gritz/v1/gritz.proto";
import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";


option go_package = "github.com/icholy/gritz/internal/proto/driver/v1;driverv1";


// DriverService is served by `gritz driver` inside the sandbox and
// called by the runner. Runs execute in-process, one at a time. The driver
// never calls the gritz server; it reports through its response log, which
// Run streams from the caller's position.
service DriverService {
  // Status reports that the server is up, plus the current run record and the
  // event cursor the runner fetches the next run's events from.
  rpc Status(StatusRequest) returns (StatusResponse);


  // Run is attach-or-start, keyed on version:
  //   another Run stream already open      -> Unavailable (retry)
  //   record.version > version             -> FailedPrecondition (stale)
  //   record.version == version            -> attach, spec ignored
  //   no record / older version, idle      -> start the run (spec required,
  //                                           NotFound without one)
  //   another version running              -> Aborted (busy)
  // At most one Run stream is open at a time. The stream first replays every
  // logged response with seq > after_seq, then follows new ones live. It ends
  // after the run's Finished has been sent. A dropped or closed stream detaches
  // and nothing else: the run keeps going, responses keep being logged, and the
  // next Run continues from whatever after_seq it brings.
  rpc Run(RunRequest) returns (stream RunResponse);


  // Stop gracefully stops the run with the given version: cancel the run
  // context with ErrStop (agents and setup commands SIGTERM their process
  // groups); the run's terminal event and Finished are logged as usual.
  // A no-op if that version is not the active run.
  rpc Stop(StopRequest) returns (StopResponse);
}


message RunRecord {
  enum State {
    STATE_UNSPECIFIED = 0;
    STATE_RUNNING = 1;
    STATE_FINISHED = 2;
  }
  int64 version = 1;
  State state = 2;
  // When the run finished. Drives the idle timeout.
  google.protobuf.Timestamp finished_at = 3;
}


message StatusRequest {}


message StatusResponse {
  // Absent if this sandbox has never started a run.
  optional RunRecord run = 1;
  // Sequence number of the last logged response. Zero if none.
  uint64 last_seq = 3;
  // ListEventsByTask page token after the last events delivered to the agent.
  // Empty before the first successful run.
  string event_token = 2;
}


// RunSpec carries everything the driver used to read from flags, its
// environment and the server.
message RunSpec {
  // The task as of this run: id, name, version, prompt, shell_session.
  gritz.v1.Task task = 1;
  // Instruction and external events after StatusResponse.event_token, fetched
  // by the runner.
  repeated gritz.v1.Event events = 2;
  // The page token after the last event above. Persisted by the driver once
  // the prompt is delivered.
  string event_token = 3;
  // The task's links. Only set on the first run.
  repeated gritz.v1.TaskLink links = 4;
  // Passed to setup commands and the agent CLI. Not set on the driver
  // process itself.
  map<string, string> env = 5;
  // Workspace secrets and the task token. Added to the run's env (except the
  // token) and masked in shipped log chunks.
  map<string, string> secrets = 6;
  // Agent config and directories. Provisioned once per sandbox, gated by
  // /gritz/.provisioned.
  repeated File files = 7;
}


message File {
  string path = 1;
  bytes data = 2;
  int64 mode = 3;
  bool dir = 4;
}


message RunRequest {
  int64 version = 1;
  // The last seq the runner has made durable on its side (taskstate's Seq).
  // Responses up to it are not replayed, and the driver may delete them.
  uint64 after_seq = 3;
  // Set to start a run. Omitted to attach.
  RunSpec spec = 2;
}


message RunResponse {
  // Response log sequence number. Set on runner_event, log_chunk and
  // finished, which are logged; zero on accepted and keep_alive, which are
  // per-stream and never stored.
  uint64 seq = 1;
  oneof event {
    // First message on every stream.
    Accepted accepted = 2;
    KeepAlive keep_alive = 3;
    // started / stopped / failed, stamped with the run's version.
    gritz.v1.RunnerEvent runner_event = 4;
    // A masked chunk of the run's log, cut at 32 KiB as today.
    LogChunk log_chunk = 5;
    // Last logged response of a run. Written after its terminal runner event.
    Finished finished = 6;
  }
}


message Accepted {
  // True if the call attached to an existing run rather than starting one.
  bool attached = 1;
}


message LogChunk {
  int64 version = 1;
  bytes data = 2;
}


message Finished {
  int64 version = 1;
}


message KeepAlive {}


message StopRequest {
  int64 version = 1;
}


message StopResponse {
  // True if a running run with this version was stopped.
  bool stopped = 1;
}
```

Everything from the runner to the driver is a unary call or the `Run` request itself, and everything back is the `Run` stream, rather than a single bidirectional stream, because Connect bidi needs HTTP/2 end to end and Lambda’s managed proxy does not provide it. Connect handlers serve the Connect, gRPC and gRPC-Web protocols on a plain `net/http` server.

The experimental Lambda backend established what the managed proxy carries. It speaks HTTP/2 to clients. The Connect and gRPC-Web protocols pass through it, but gRPC does not, so the runner’s driver client uses Connect, connect-go’s default, on every backend. Server streams are not buffered: each `RunResponse` reaches the runner as the driver writes it. The proxy cut a stream that had been idle for 15 minutes. `KeepAlive` every 15 seconds keeps a stream well inside that limit, so the idle cut never applies to a `Run` stream.

### The driver server

[Section titled “The driver server”](#the-driver-server)

`gritz driver [--addr :8080 | unix:///path]` is the driver server and the sandbox entrypoint; the one-shot `gritz driver --task` is gone. It holds no task identity and no server credentials of its own; everything arrives in `Run`.

**Per-run construction.** What `internal/command/driver.go` builds once per process today moves into the `Run` handler, and the server calls go away:

| Today                                                        | Driver server                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--server` / `--task` / `--token` flags                      | `RunSpec.task`; no `gritzclient`                                                                                             |
| `GetTask` at the top of `Driver.Run`                         | `RunSpec.task` (the runner already holds it from its poll)                                                                   |
| `drainEvents` (`ListEventsByTask` from `cfg.NextEventToken`) | `RunSpec.events`, fetched by the runner from `StatusResponse.event_token`                                                    |
| `ListLinks` on the first run                                 | `RunSpec.links`                                                                                                              |
| `SubmitRunnerEvents` for started / stopped / failed          | logged `runner_event` responses                                                                                              |
| `logship.Shipper` calling `AppendLogChunk`                   | the shipper’s sender logs `log_chunk` responses; masking and chunk cutting are unchanged                                     |
| `driverSecrets()` reads `GRITZ_SECRETS` via `os.Getenv`      | `RunSpec.secrets`; the `redact.Writer` is built per run before the first byte                                                |
| `agent.OpenDriverLog` once                                   | opened per run, still appending to `/gritz/log`                                                                              |
| SIGTERM handler in `Driver.Run`                              | run context cancelled with `ErrStop` by `Stop`; SIGTERM to the server process means shut down (stopping an active run first) |
| exit code means “did the driver report?”                     | the response log: the terminal event is durable in the sandbox before `Finished`                                             |

The event cursor stays in the driver’s config (`cfg.NextEventToken`). The driver saves `RunSpec.event_token` there after `a.Prompt` returns, as `drainEvents`’ result is saved today, and reports it in `Status`. The at-least-once delivery of events to the agent is unchanged.

**Per-run environment.** Nothing may inherit the process environment, because secrets arrive over RPC. `agent.Driver` gains an `Env []string` field, threaded to:

* `agent/claude.go:72` and `agent/cursor.go:63` (`os.Environ()` today)
* `agent/codex.go`, `agent/copilot.go`, `agent/sloppy.go` (nil `cmd.Env` today, which inherits)
* setup commands, `agent/driver.go:288`
* `os.ExpandEnv(cfg.Cwd)`, `agent/driver.go:226`, which becomes `os.Expand` over the run env

**Response log.** `/gritz/responses/<version>.log`, one append-only file per run of length-delimited `RunResponse` messages, each fsynced before it is streamed. Responses are appended in the order the driver produces them, so a run’s log chunks and runner events interleave as they happened. Sequence numbers are monotonic for the life of the sandbox, not per run, so a tail of an earlier run that the runner has not yet stored is replayed before a new run’s responses. The driver deletes a version’s file once a `Run` arrives with an `after_seq` at or past that version’s `Finished`; in practice, the previous run’s file goes when the next run starts.

**Run record.** `/gritz/run.json`, written atomically with `internal/x/atomicio`:

* `{version, running}` before a run starts;
* `{version, finished, finished_at}` after the run’s `Finished` is logged.

On boot, a record still `running` means the process died mid-run. Before serving, the driver logs a `failed` runner event (“driver restarted mid-run”) and a `Finished` for that version, and rewrites the record as finished. The runner learns about the crash through the log like any other outcome. The record and the response log live on the sandbox’s disk, so they survive driver restarts and parking, but not sandbox loss.

**Server rules.**

* At most one run at a time. A `Run` that starts a new version while an older run has responses after `after_seq` is allowed; the stream replays them first.
* At most one `Run` stream at a time. A second `Run` while one is open is rejected with `Unavailable`, so there is only ever one reader of the log.
* A dropped stream is routine, not a failure. Proxies time out, tokens expire, runners restart. The run’s context is independent of any request’s context: the driver detaches the stream, keeps running the agent, keeps logging responses, and serves the next `Run` exactly as if it had stayed connected. Only `Stop` and the server’s own shutdown cancel a run.
* The driver notices a dead stream when a write to it fails. `KeepAlive` is sent every 15 seconds, so a stream whose runner has gone away is released within that interval and the next `Run` is accepted.

**Authentication.** The driver takes an optional runner public key from `GRITZ_RUNNER_PUBLIC_KEY` or `/gritz/runner.pub`, read on boot. The key is a raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key encoded as unpadded base64url, 43 characters, so it fits any channel a backend has. JWTs are signed with EdDSA.

* **Key present:** every request must carry `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`, signed by the runner’s key, with `sub` set to the task id and a short expiry. The driver verifies it against the key and rejects a `sub` other than the task of its first `Run`.
* **No key:** the API is unauthenticated.

Whether a sandbox needs the driver’s own auth is the backend’s decision, and setting it up is part of `Create`. A backend whose platform authenticates the path to the sandbox per sandbox or per port (Lambda’s IAM-gated managed proxy, AgentCore) installs no key. A backend whose platform does not, or only with an account-wide credential, writes the runner’s public key through a channel only it controls:

| Backend         | Platform auth on the path | Key delivery               |
| --------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Lambda MicroVMs | IAM, per VM and port      | none                       |
| AgentCore       | IAM                       | none                       |
| Docker          | none                      | env at create              |
| DigitalOcean    | none documented           | env at create              |
| Nomad           | none without Consul mTLS  | job env                    |
| Firecracker     | none                      | MMDS or `config.tar`       |
| Fly Sprites     | the org-wide API token    | fs API, right after create |
| exe.dev         | SSH (port-forward)        | SFTP                       |

The key is public, so an agent that reads it gains nothing. The runner keeps one Ed25519 key pair in its state directory and puts the public half in every `Spec` (`RunnerPublicKey`); the backend installs it or ignores it. The runner signs a JWT and passes it to `Dial` regardless of backend: a driver with no key ignores the header, so the runner never needs to know which kind of sandbox it is talking to, and the backend never holds the signing key. The JWT’s expiry bounds the client’s lifetime; the runner dials again when it expires or when a call returns `Unauthenticated`. A `Run` stream is checked once, when it opens, so a long run keeps its stream.

On every backend the agent inside the sandbox can reach the driver on localhost without going through the platform’s path, and with no key the driver does not stop it. That is the same trust boundary as the agent’s existing ability to rewrite the response log or kill the driver.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Platform
    participant D as Driver server
    participant F as Sandbox disk


    P->>D: start process
    D->>F: read /gritz/run.json
    alt state = running (process died mid-run)
        D->>F: log += failed(version), Finished(version)
        D->>F: write {version, finished, finished_at: now}
    else finished / absent
        Note over D,F: keep as is
    end
    D->>D: serve
```

### Backend interface

[Section titled “Backend interface”](#backend-interface)

The backend is split in two. A `Backend` creates sandboxes and reopens recorded ones; a `Sandbox` is a reference to one provisioned sandbox and manages it. The runner speaks the driver protocol over the client `Sandbox.Dial` returns.

```go
// Backend creates task sandboxes on a concrete runtime and reopens recorded
// ones. It never speaks the driver protocol.
type Backend interface {
  ValidateWorkspace(ws *workspace.Workspace) error


  // Create provisions a sandbox for spec without starting it, and returns as
  // soon as the platform has assigned it an identity. On error no sandbox
  // exists: a backend whose provisioning fails after the platform assigned an
  // identity (Docker's binary copy) destroys what it created, on a context
  // of its own, before returning the error.
  Create(ctx context.Context, spec *Spec) (Sandbox, error)


  // Open rehydrates a sandbox from a handle that Sandbox.Handle returned. It
  // does no I/O and does not check that the sandbox still exists; a gone
  // sandbox shows up on the returned Sandbox's methods. It fails only for a
  // handle this backend cannot decode (another type, malformed Data).
  Open(h Handle) (Sandbox, error)


  Close() error
}


// Sandbox is a reference to one provisioned sandbox, in whatever state it is
// in: created, running, parked or gone. It holds the per-sandbox state its
// backend needs (the Docker container ID, the Lambda endpoint and cached proxy
// token). Its methods are safe for concurrent use.
//
// A Sandbox can be stale: the platform may have destroyed the sandbox since
// Create or Open. Every method handles that: Status reports Gone, Start and
// Park return ErrGone, and Destroy returns nil.
type Sandbox interface {
  // Handle identifies the sandbox for taskstate/. It is fixed at Create and
  // never changes over the sandbox's life.
  Handle() Handle


  // Start boots a created sandbox or resumes a parked one, and blocks until
  // the platform reports it running. Starting a running sandbox is a no-op. A
  // gone sandbox returns ErrGone; a sandbox in a transitional state
  // (SUSPENDING, pausing) returns a plain error. Start never creates a sandbox.
  Start(ctx context.Context) error


  // Dial returns a client for the sandbox's driver server. Every call it makes
  // carries jwt as a bearer token, plus any platform credentials (Lambda's
  // port-scoped proxy token). A driver with no runner key ignores the JWT.
  // Dial does not wait for the driver; readiness is the runner's Status
  // polling.
  Dial(ctx context.Context, jwt string) (driverv1connect.DriverServiceClient, error)


  // Status reports the platform's view of the sandbox: Up, Parked or Gone.
  // Created but never started, and transitional states (SUSPENDING, pausing),
  // report Parked.
  Status(ctx context.Context) (Status, error)


  // Park stops compute while preserving the sandbox, blocking until the
  // platform reports the stable parked state. Parking a parked sandbox is a
  // no-op.
  Park(ctx context.Context) error


  // Destroy deletes the sandbox. Destroying a gone sandbox is not an error.
  Destroy(ctx context.Context) error
}
```

`Create` and `Start` are separate because both platforms the design targets return an identity before the sandbox boots: Docker’s `ContainerCreate` returns the container ID, and Lambda’s `RunMicrovm` returns the microVM ID while the VM is still pending. One `Start` covers both a fresh boot and a resume, so the runner’s start path is the same whether or not the sandbox has run before.

The runner’s rule follows: record `sb.Handle()` in `taskstate/` as soon as `Create` returns, before anything else can fail.

```go
sb, err := r.backend.Create(ctx, spec)
if err != nil {
  return err
}
r.record(task, sb.Handle())
if err := sb.Start(ctx); err != nil {
  return err // the record stays; a later Start or Remove deals with it
}
```

A record now always exists for a sandbox that failed to come up (a boot timeout, a failed start, a cancelled context), so a later `Start` retries it and `Remove` destroys it. A backend that cannot provide an identity before boot (most VM and sandbox APIs create and boot in one call) implements `Create` as that call plus the wait, and its `Start` on a fresh sandbox is a no-op; it keeps the window of open question 10. So does a `Create` whose cleanup after a failed provisioning step itself fails.

The runner holds a `Sandbox` per tracked task, next to its lock and idle timer, from `Create`, or from `Open` on the recorded handle when it does not have one (`Load`, a follow-up `Start`). Because `Open` does no I/O, the runner never needs the platform to reach a record.

The split has two costs. A `Sandbox` the runner holds can go stale: a sandbox pruned, removed by hand or reclaimed by the platform is only noticed on the next call, so every method has to handle gone rather than assume the sandbox `Create` or `Open` saw. And `Sandbox` methods are called concurrently: by `supervise` (`Dial` and `Status` while reconnecting, outside the lock, because it holds the stream for the whole run), by `Kill` (`Dial`), and by the idle-park timer (`Dial`, `Park`). The per-task lock serializes the lifecycle calls (`Start`, `Park`, `Destroy`), but not `supervise`’s, so an implementation’s cached state (Lambda’s endpoint and proxy token) needs its own synchronization.

`Spec` shrinks to what the platform needs to create the sandbox: `TaskID`, `Workspace`, and `RunnerPublicKey`, which the backend installs in the sandbox only if its platform does not authenticate the path (see Authentication). `Cmd`, `Env` and `Files` move into `RunSpec`. `Launch`, `Probe`, `Signal`, `Wait` and `ExitCode` are removed.

### Runner

[Section titled “Runner”](#runner)

`runner.go` takes over what the backend used to hide. A per-task lock serializes `Start`, `Kill`, `Remove` and the idle park, and with them every `Sandbox.Start`, `Park` and `Destroy`; `supervise` runs outside it (see Backend interface).

The driver-server backends showed two problems with today’s `Launch` that this split fixes:

* **`Launch` blocks `Poll`.** The backends’ `Launch` waits for the driver (`waitReady`, polling `Status` for up to 30s on Docker, 1m on Lambda) and starts the run before returning, and `Poll` waits for every `Start` in its pass. A slow sandbox therefore delays the next poll, and with it every other task’s start and stop commands. Here `Create` and `Sandbox.Start` only wait for the platform; the `Status` wait and `Run` move out of the poll pass into the task’s own goroutine, after the handle is recorded.
* **`waitReady` counts the image entrypoint’s time.** The readiness timeout starts when the platform reports the sandbox running, so whatever the image’s entrypoint does before it execs the driver eats into the budget for the driver to answer. The runner’s readiness wait needs a budget that covers the entrypoint explicitly (open question 8).

| Runner method  | With the driver server                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Start(task)`  | Under the lock. With no record: `backend.Create(spec)`, then write `sb.Handle()` to `taskstate/`. With one: the task’s `Sandbox`, or `backend.Open` on the recorded handle. Then `sb.Start()`; `ErrGone` → remove the record and fail, any other error → keep the record and fail. Then `sb.Dial`, poll `Status` with backoff (timeout → error). A running record for this version: a no-op. Otherwise fetch events after `Status.event_token` (and links on the first run), mint the task token, `Run(version, spec, after_seq: record.Seq)` until `Accepted`, cancel any idle timer, and hand the stream to `supervise`.                          |
| `supervise`    | Reads the stream. `runner_event` → enqueue on the runner event outbox; `log_chunk` → `AppendLogChunk`; then advance the record’s `Seq` (batched). `Finished` for the task’s current version → release the slot, arm the idle timer, return. A dropped stream is expected: re-dial and `Run(version, after_seq: Seq)` straight away, no recovery check, retrying `Unavailable` (the driver has not yet released the old stream) with backoff. Only when reconnecting keeps failing: `sb.Status`; gone → failed backstop and remove the record; parked → failed backstop; up → keep retrying until the readiness timeout (timeout → failed backstop). |
| `Load`         | For each record: `backend.Open(handle)`, then `sb.Status`; gone → as today; parked → `failIfTaskRunning`; up → `sb.Dial`, `Run(version, after_seq: record.Seq)` to attach. The replay delivers whatever the previous runner process missed, including a `Finished` it never saw.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `Running`      | `sb.Status` up and `Status` reports a running record for this version.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `Kill(task)`   | Under the lock: `sb.Dial`, `Stop(version)`; `signalled = stopped`. The terminal event arrives through the stream.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `Remove(task)` | Under the lock: cancel the idle timer, `sb.Destroy` (opening the record if needed), remove the record.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `Prune`        | Unchanged, on top of `backend.Open` and `sb.Status`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

The failed backstop is now only for sandbox loss and an unreachable driver. A driver crash is reported by the restarted driver through its response log, and a run that finished while the runner was down is reported when the runner reattaches.

**Position.** The runner’s position in a sandbox’s response log is a `Seq` field on its `taskstate/` record: the last sequence number that is durable on the runner’s side. A runner event is durable once `Enqueue` returns (the runner’s outbox delivers it to the server), a log chunk once `AppendLogChunk` succeeds. Responses are processed in order, so a failed `AppendLogChunk` is retried with backoff before later responses; a permanent failure drops the chunk and moves on. `supervise` writes `Seq` in batches and after every runner event, under the task’s lock, rewriting the record it read so a concurrent `Start` and `supervise` never lose each other’s fields. A runner that crashes after delivering a response but before writing `Seq` delivers it again on reattach. The server’s version guard already absorbs a repeated runner event. Repeated log chunks are an open question. A record from before this change has no `Seq`, which reads as 0: replay everything the driver still has.

**Event fetching.** The runner fetches the run’s events with `ListEventsByTask` from `Status.event_token`, filtered to the instruction and external types, exactly as `drainEvents` does today, and the links with `ListLinks` on the first run (`Status.event_token` empty and no run record).

### Idle parking

[Section titled “Idle parking”](#idle-parking)

`Workspace` gains a backend-agnostic field:

```yaml
workspaces:
  pets-workshop:
    idle_timeout: 5m   # default 0: park as soon as the run finishes
```

When `supervise` sees `Finished`, the runner arms a timer for `idle_timeout`. When it fires, it takes the task’s lock and checks the driver’s `Status`: it calls `sb.Park` only if the record is finished, `finished_at + idle_timeout` has passed, and the record’s `Seq` has reached `Status.last_seq`, so everything the driver logged is stored on the runner’s side. A `Start` that won the lock in between is never undone. With an idle timeout of 0 this is today’s behavior. `Load` re-derives timers from `finished_at` for sandboxes that are up and idle.

The semaphore slot is released on `Finished`, not when the sandbox parks, so warm sandboxes never block new runs. The idle timeout is the only bound on what warm sandboxes cost.

If the runner restarts mid-park, the next `Start` may find the sandbox in a transitional state. `sb.Start` returns a plain error: the run fails, the taskstate record is kept, and a later start or archive proceeds normally.

### Platform implementations

[Section titled “Platform implementations”](#platform-implementations)

|           | Docker                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Lambda MicroVMs                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Create`  | `ContainerCreate` with `Cmd: [BinaryPath, "driver"]`, `GRITZ_RUNNER_PUBLIC_KEY=spec.RunnerPublicKey` in `Env`, labels as today; tar-copy the prebuilt binary. A failed copy removes the container. Handle: the container ID.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | `RunMicrovm` with no run-hook payload; returns as soon as the call does, with the VM still `PENDING`. Handle: the microVM ID and the endpoint `RunMicrovm` returns.                                           |
| `Open`    | decode the handle                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | decode the handle; the port-scoped proxy token is minted on first use and cached on the `Sandbox`                                                                                                             |
| `Start`   | `ContainerStart` (a no-op on a running container); not found → `ErrGone`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | poll `GetMicrovm`: `PENDING` → poll until `RUNNING`; `RUNNING` → no-op; `SUSPENDED` → `ResumeMicrovm`, poll until `RUNNING`; `SUSPENDING` → plain error; `TERMINATING`, `TERMINATED` or not found → `ErrGone` |
| `Dial`    | client whose transport tunnels each connection through a Docker exec of `gritz tool proxy --addr unix:///gritz/driver.sock` (stdin/stdout attached, stdout demultiplexed with `stdcopy`), adding the JWT. The driver listens on that unix socket inside the container, not on a port, so any network mode works and nothing outside the container reaches it over the network. The runner needs only Docker API access, never a network route to the container. | Connect client for the managed proxy endpoint over HTTP/2, adding a cached, minted port-scoped token and the JWT                                                                                              |
| `Status`  | inspect: running → Up, created or exited → Parked, not found → Gone                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | `GetMicrovm`: `RUNNING` → Up; `PENDING`, `SUSPENDING`, `SUSPENDED` → Parked; `TERMINATING`, `TERMINATED` or not found → Gone                                                                                  |
| `Park`    | `docker stop` with an explicit timeout covering a graceful server shutdown; not found → `ErrGone`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `SuspendMicrovm`, then poll until `SUSPENDED`; `TERMINATING`, `TERMINATED` or not found → `ErrGone`                                                                                                           |
| `Destroy` | `ContainerRemove` (force); not found → nil                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `TerminateMicrovm`; already terminating, terminated or not found → nil                                                                                                                                        |

On both platforms the agent files (agent config and directories) travel in `RunSpec.files` and the driver writes them, so no backend copies files into the sandbox. Docker still copies the prebuilt binary.

Lambda changes, all in place in the Lambda backend (`internal/runner/backend/lambdamicrovm`):

* The image entrypoint (`microvm.Dockerfile`) is `gritz driver --aws-lambda-hooks`. The flag mounts `awsmicrovm.Handler` with nil funcs on `awsmicrovm.HookPort`, which acknowledges every hook with 200. No hook does work.
* The run spec travels in `Run` over the proxy, so the backend needs no `Stager`, `awsmvm.S3Stager`, `LambdaMicroVM.StagingBucket` or S3 permission on the execution role.
* No shim runs in the VM. Removing the old backend (L1) deletes `internal/runner/microvmshim`, `gritz tool microvm-shim`, the stager and the `staging_bucket` field.

### Sequences

[Section titled “Sequences”](#sequences)

Start:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as gritz Server
    participant R as Runner
    participant T as taskstate/
    participant P as Backend / Platform
    participant D as Driver server
    participant F as Sandbox disk


    R->>R: lock(task)
    alt no record
        R->>P: Create(spec)
        P->>P: create, until the platform assigns an identity
        P-->>R: sb
        R->>T: write {version, sb.Handle()}
    else recorded
        R->>P: Open(handle) (no I/O)
        P-->>R: sb
    end
    R->>P: sb.Start()
    P->>P: boot / resume, wait until running
    alt gone
        P-->>R: ErrGone
        R->>T: remove record
    else transitional or failed
        P-->>R: error (record kept)
    end
    P-->>R: nil
    R->>P: sb.Dial(jwt)
    loop until the driver answers (backoff, timeout -> error)
        R->>D: Status()
    end
    D-->>R: {run, event_token}
    R->>S: ListEventsByTask(event_token), ListLinks (first run)
    R->>S: CreateTaskToken
    R->>D: Run(version, spec, after_seq: Seq)
    alt record.version > version
        D-->>R: FailedPrecondition (stale)
    else record.version == version
        D-->>R: Accepted{attached: true}
    else no record or older, idle
        D->>F: write {version, running}
        D->>D: provision files (marker-gated)
        D->>D: build log, shipper, secret mask
        D-->>R: Accepted{attached: false}
        D->>F: log += started(version)
    else another version running
        D-->>R: Aborted (busy)
    end
    R->>R: cancel idle timer, unlock, supervise(stream)
```

Supervise:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as gritz Server
    participant O as Runner outbox
    participant T as taskstate/
    participant R as Runner
    participant P as Backend / Platform
    participant D as Driver server
    participant F as Sandbox disk


    loop until Finished(version)
        D->>F: log += response
        D-->>R: RunResponse{seq, ...}
        alt runner_event
            R->>O: Enqueue
            O->>S: SubmitRunnerEvents
        else log_chunk
            R->>S: AppendLogChunk
        end
        R->>T: Seq = seq (batched)
        opt stream dropped (routine)
            Note over D: run continues, responses keep being logged
            R->>P: sb.Dial(jwt)
            R->>D: Run(version, after_seq: Seq) (attach, replay)
            opt Unavailable (old stream not yet released)
                R->>D: retry Run with backoff
            end
            opt reconnecting keeps failing
                R->>P: sb.Status()
                alt gone / parked
                    R->>O: Enqueue failed (backstop)
                else up
                    R->>D: keep retrying (readiness timeout -> backstop)
                end
            end
        end
    end
    R->>R: release slot, arm idle timer
```

Runner crash and reattach:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Runner (new process)
    participant T as taskstate/
    participant P as Backend / Platform
    participant D as Driver server
    participant F as Sandbox disk


    Note over D,F: run continued; responses logged past the runner's Seq
    R->>T: list records {version, handle, Seq: n}
    R->>P: Open(handle) (no I/O)
    P-->>R: sb
    R->>P: sb.Status()
    P-->>R: Up
    R->>P: sb.Dial(jwt)
    R->>D: Run(version, after_seq: n)
    D->>F: read log after n
    D-->>R: Accepted{attached: true}
    D-->>R: RunResponse{seq: n+1}, RunResponse{seq: n+2}, ...
    Note over R,D: then live responses, as in Supervise
```

Kill:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Runner
    participant P as Backend / Platform
    participant D as Driver server
    participant F as Sandbox disk


    R->>R: lock(task)
    R->>P: sb.Dial(jwt)
    R->>D: Stop(version)
    alt version is the active run
        D->>D: cancel run context (ErrStop)
        D->>D: agent / setup process groups get SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after WaitDelay
        D->>F: log += stopped(version), Finished(version)
        D-->>R: stopped: true
    else not running / other version / unreachable
        D-->>R: stopped: false
    end
    R->>R: unlock
    Note over R,D: stopped and Finished arrive on the supervise stream
```

Idle park:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Runner
    participant P as Backend / Platform
    participant D as Driver server


    Note over R: timer armed on Finished, or re-derived by Load from finished_at
    R->>R: timer fires, lock(task)
    R->>P: sb.Dial(jwt)
    R->>D: Status()
    alt run active, Seq < last_seq, or idle_timeout not elapsed
        Note over R: skip
    else finished and idle long enough
        R->>P: sb.Park() (blocks until stable)
        alt Docker
            P->>D: docker stop: SIGTERM, server shuts down, container exits
        else Lambda
            P->>P: SuspendMicrovm, poll until SUSPENDED
        end
    end
    R->>R: unlock
```

### What doesn’t change

[Section titled “What doesn’t change”](#what-doesnt-change)

The runner event outbox, the server, the database schema, the task state machine, and `gritz.proto`. The taskstate store gains only the `Seq` field. The terminal event’s meaning is unchanged: the driver decides `started`, `stopped` and `failed`, and the server’s version guard drops a stale one. Only the path changes, from driver → server to driver response log → runner outbox → server.

## Implementation Plan

[Section titled “Implementation Plan”](#implementation-plan)

The design lands in three stages: an experimental phase that proved the driver server on both platforms (done), a switch-over that makes it the only path, and the `Backend` interface redesign on top. Every step merges on its own and leaves a working system.

### Phase A: the driver server behind experimental backends (done)

[Section titled “Phase A: the driver server behind experimental backends (done)”](#phase-a-the-driver-server-behind-experimental-backends-done)

Phase A changed the driver’s process model and nothing else. The driver server still talks to the gritz server directly, exactly as the one-shot driver does, so today’s `backend.Backend` interface (`Launch`, `Wait`, `Probe`, `Signal`, `Destroy`) keeps its meaning: `Wait` still answers “did the driver report?”. No idle parking, no runner key.

It delivered:

* `agent.Driver.Env`, threaded to every agent CLI, setup commands and `Cwd` expansion.
* `proto/driver/v1/driver.proto`, first cut: `Status`, `Run` and `Stop`. `RunSpec` carries what the one-shot driver reads from flags and its environment (`task_id`, `server_url`, `token`, `env`, `secrets`) plus the agent files (`files`); `RunResponse` carries `accepted`, `keep_alive` and `finished`, whose `Finished` has a `reported` bool.
* The run record (`/gritz/run.json`) with boot reconciliation.
* `gritz driver --serve`: attach-or-start keyed on version, one `Run` stream at a time, a dropped stream leaves the run going, `Stop` cancels with `ErrStop`, the agent files provisioned once per sandbox behind `/gritz/.provisioned`.
* The `experimentaldocker` backend (handle type `experimental-docker`), now `docker` (L2), reaching the driver through a Docker exec tunnel of `gritz tool proxy`, and stopping the container after every run.
* The `experimentallambdamicrovm` backend (handle type `experimental-lambda-microvm`), now `lambdamicrovm` (L2): the driver server as the VM’s main process, acknowledging the Lambda hooks with `--aws-lambda-hooks`, reached through the managed proxy with a cached port-scoped token, the run spec in `Run` instead of S3, and the VM suspended (polled until `SUSPENDED`) after every run. Its resume returns a plain error for `SUSPENDING`, which fixes problem 3 once the old backend is gone.
* `--backend experimental-docker` and `--backend experimental-lambda-microvm` (removed in L2, replaced by `docker` and `lambda-microvm`). Each replaced its old counterpart rather than running beside it: handles of any other type are treated as gone.

It left the Docker driver listening on `:8080`, so sibling containers on a shared bridge could reach it and the host, `container:` and `none` network modes were rejected; L1.5 moves it to a unix socket. It leaves open that a sandbox keeps the driver binary it was created with, so `driver.v1` changes must stay wire-compatible.

What it established is recorded in the design: the exec tunnel (Platform implementations, open question 3), the managed proxy’s protocol behavior (Service definition), and the two problems with `Launch` that the interface redesign fixes (Runner).

### Switch-over

[Section titled “Switch-over”](#switch-over)

The driver-server backends replace the old ones, still on today’s `backend.Backend` interface. There is no migration: tasks on the old backends are archived before upgrading (open question 4).

* **L1: remove the old backends** (#1711) — Delivers: deletion of the old `docker` and `lambdamicrovm` backends, `internal/runner/microvmshim`, `gritz tool microvm-shim`, the S3 `Stager` / `awsmvm.S3Stager`, and the `staging_bucket` workspace field. `--backend` accepts only the experimental backends. Depends on: Phase A. Verifiable by: build and tests.
* **L1.5: serve the Docker driver on a unix socket** (#1719) — Delivers: `gritz driver --serve --addr` and `gritz tool proxy --addr` accept `unix:///path`; the Docker backend starts the driver on `unix:///gritz/driver.sock` and tunnels to it, and accepts every network mode. The Lambda backend keeps TCP `:8080`, which the managed proxy routes to. Depends on: L1. Verifiable by: the runner integration test on `network_mode: host`.
* **L2: promote the experimental backends** (#1712) — Delivers: `experimentaldocker` renamed to `docker` and `experimentallambdamicrovm` to `lambdamicrovm`. The handle types become `docker` and `lambda-microvm`, a clean break: handles of the `experimental-*` types are treated as gone. The `--backend` values become `docker` (the default) and `lambda-microvm`; any other value, `experimental-docker` and `experimental-lambda-microvm` included, is an error. READMEs, the dev compose file and the docs are updated. Depends on: L1. Verifiable by: a runner with the default backend running a task end to end.
* **L3: remove the one-shot driver** (#1713) — Delivers: `gritz driver` becomes the driver server (no `--serve` flag), and the one-shot plumbing goes: `backend.Spec.Cmd`, and the driver environment the backends turn back into a `RunSpec`. Depends on: L2. Verifiable by: build and tests, and a task running end to end on Docker.

### Backend interface redesign

[Section titled “Backend interface redesign”](#backend-interface-redesign)

After the switch-over, the rest of the design lands on the promoted backends. These steps are split into their own layers when they become current; the order is:

1. **Driver inputs and outputs behind interfaces** — `agent.Driver` takes the task, events and links as inputs and reports runner events and log chunks through a sink, implemented with `gritzclient` so behavior is unchanged.
2. **Response log** — the per-version `RunResponse` log with read-after-seq and deletion behind a position; `RunRequest.after_seq`, `StatusResponse.last_seq`, and the `runner_event` and `log_chunk` cases.
3. **`Backend` / `Sandbox` interfaces and runner path** — the interfaces from the design (`Backend`: `ValidateWorkspace`, `Create`, `Open`, `Close`; `Sandbox`: `Handle`, `Start`, `Dial`, `Status`, `Park`, `Destroy`), the runner recording `sb.Handle()` right after `Create`, `runner.go` speaking the driver protocol (`Start`, `supervise` forwarding and advancing `Seq`, `Load`, `Kill`, `Remove`), `taskstate.Record.Seq`, both backends moved onto it with the driver reporting through the response log, and `Launch`, `Wait`, `Probe`, `Signal` and `ExitCode` removed. This is where `Launch` stops blocking `Poll` and the readiness wait stops counting the entrypoint (see Runner). Verifiable by: runner tests against a fake backend and an in-memory driver server, including a runner restart mid-run and a `Start` that fails after `Create` (the record is kept and `Remove` destroys the sandbox).
4. **Runner key** — the runner’s key pair, `Spec.RunnerPublicKey`, `Dial(jwt)`, and JWT verification in the driver when it has a key. Docker installs the key.
5. **Idle parking** — `Workspace.IdleTimeout` (default 0, today’s behavior), the runner’s idle timers and `Park`. Docker parks with `docker stop` and Lambda with `SuspendMicrovm` instead of after every run.

## Trade-offs

[Section titled “Trade-offs”](#trade-offs)

**Driver as server vs. a shim.** A shim (today’s `microvmshim`, or the generic shim proposal) keeps the driver one-shot and isolates each run in its own process, which gives a fresh environment, a real exit code and crash containment for free. The cost is a second in-sandbox component, a supervisor contract, and for the generic shim a second release artifact. Making the driver the server removes all of that; the price is the per-run refactor of the driver and a weaker failure mode, below.

**In-process runs vs. a child process per run.** A server that spawns `gritz driver run` per `Run` would keep today’s driver unchanged, but it is the shim’s supervisor role folded into the gritz binary rather than removed. In-process runs mean a panic in one run kills the server: the restarted driver reports the run as failed from its run record, but the real exit code is gone.

**Driver reports through the runner vs. directly to the server.** Routing everything through the runner means the sandbox needs no route to the server for the driver’s own traffic, the runner sees every outcome first-hand (no exit-code signalling, no race between the driver’s report and the runner’s backstop), and the server’s inputs come from one component. The cost is that the runner is now on the path of every log byte, and a runner that is down delays (but does not lose) the driver’s reports until it reattaches.

**Runner-held position vs. driver-held acks.** With an outbox and an `Ack` RPC the driver would track delivery, and the runner would persist nothing per message. With the position in `taskstate/`, the driver keeps no state about its reader, there is one RPC fewer, every reconnect is the same `Run(version, after_seq)`, and the log is an exact history of the run that any reader can replay. The cost is a `taskstate/` write per batch, the coordination between `Start` and `supervise` on the record, and at-least-once delivery for whatever was delivered after the last `Seq` write when the runner crashes.

**Runner owns the driver protocol vs. a `DriverBackend` adapter.** An adapter would keep `runner.go` unchanged behind the old `Launch`/`Wait`/`Probe` interface, but `Launch` could only return the handle after the run started, and the log replay would be hidden behind `Wait`. With a sandbox-only `Backend` and `Sandbox`, the handle is persisted as soon as `Create` returns, before the sandbox boots, and the runner deals with runs directly. The cost is a larger change to `runner.go` and its tests.

**Idle timer in the runner vs. the driver or the platform.** The driver knows idleness exactly but holds no platform credentials, and on Lambda or DigitalOcean a process exit does not park. Platform idle policies (Lambda `idlePolicy`, DigitalOcean `auto_pause`) judge idleness by activity, not by “no active run”, so a quiet agent could be parked mid-run; Lambda’s minimum is also 600s. The runner has both the knowledge (`Status`) and the credentials (via the backend).

**Separate `Create` and `Start` vs. one `Start` returning a handle with its error.** A single `Start(spec, reuse)` that creates, boots and returns the handle alongside any error would fit platforms that create and boot in one blocking call, and covers every failure the backend can observe. But the runner learns the handle only when `Start` returns, so a runner that crashes during a boot leaks the sandbox, and every call site has to remember to persist a handle that came back with an error. Both platforms the design targets return an identity before boot (`ContainerCreate`, `RunMicrovm`), so `Create` can return as soon as the sandbox exists, and the runner records the handle before anything else can fail; the window that remains is the platform call itself. Splitting `Sandbox` from `Backend` also gives per-sandbox state (the Docker container ID, Lambda’s endpoint and proxy token) one place to live instead of being decoded from the handle on every call. The costs: a `Sandbox` can be stale, so every method has to handle a sandbox that is gone; `Sandbox` methods are called concurrently by `supervise`, `Kill` and the idle-park timer, so implementations must be safe for concurrent use where the runner’s per-task lock does not cover them; and a platform with no identity before boot implements `Create` as create-and-boot, keeping the window open question 10 asks about.

**Server streaming plus unary calls vs. bidirectional streaming.** A bidi `Run` would carry `Stop` and the runner’s position on the same stream, but needs HTTP/2 end to end, which Lambda’s managed proxy does not provide: it speaks HTTP/2 to clients, but gRPC does not pass through it. A server stream works through it unbuffered, which is all `Run` needs.

**Connect vs. grpc-go.** Connect handlers are plain `net/http`, already used throughout the codebase, and serve Connect, gRPC and gRPC-Web from one handler. That turned out to matter: the Lambda managed proxy passes Connect and gRPC-Web but not gRPC, so a grpc-go server would not have been reachable through it.

**Docker exec tunnel vs. a network path.** Reaching the driver through a Docker exec of `gritz tool proxy` costs an exec per connection, and the runner’s connection depends on the Docker daemon’s stream handling. In exchange the runner needs only Docker API access: it does not care which networks the container is on, whether the runner itself runs in a container, or whether `DOCKER_HOST` is remote. Because the tunnel connects from inside the container, the driver needs no port at all: it listens on a unix socket in the container’s filesystem, `/gritz/driver.sock` (#1719). Sibling containers on a shared network cannot reach it, and drivers sharing a network namespace (`network_mode: host` or `container:`) do not collide, so every network mode works. A published port and a unix socket bind-mounted out to the runner were tried and abandoned (#1697).

## Open Questions

[Section titled “Open Questions”](#open-questions)

1. **Agent MCP and shell relay.** The injected `gritz tool agent-mcp` server and the debug-shell relay (`shell.Serve`) still dial the server with the task token. Are they in scope? The MCP tools are request/response, which the `Run` stream cannot carry; they would need their own RPC on the driver that the runner proxies, or keep going direct.
2. **Duplicate log chunks.** A chunk delivered after the last `Seq` write before a runner crash is appended twice. Should `AppendLogChunkRequest` gain a sequence number the server deduplicates on, or is a rare repeated chunk acceptable?
3. **Docker reachability.** Resolved in Phase A (#1697): the runner never connects to the container over the network. Each driver connection is tunnelled through a Docker exec of `gritz tool proxy --addr unix:///gritz/driver.sock`, which copies its stdin to the driver and the driver to its stdout, so the runner needs only Docker API access — it works for a runner in a container, a container on several networks, and a remote `DOCKER_HOST`. A published port and a unix socket bind-mounted out to the runner were tried and abandoned.
4. **Migrating existing sandboxes.** Resolved: no migration. Tasks on the old backends are archived before upgrading to the switch-over (L1), and the experimental handle types are a clean break at L2: a handle of any type the backend does not own is treated as gone. After the switch-over, the redesign steps must keep `driver.v1` wire-compatible, or the affected sandboxes be recreated, because a sandbox keeps the driver binary it was created with (see question 5).
5. **Driver revalidation.** A sandbox that stays up across a gritz release keeps serving with the old driver. Should `Status` report the driver version so the runner can park and restart stale drivers between runs?
6. **Lambda process exit.** What does Lambda do when the main process of a running MicroVM exits (a driver crash)? If the VM stays `RUNNING`, the health timeout covers it, but `Start` has no way to restart the process; should the runner destroy it and treat it as gone?
7. **Response log size.** A version’s log is only deleted when the next run starts, so a long run, or a runner that stays down, leaves it growing with log chunks. Should the driver cap it (dropping the oldest log chunks, never runner events)?
8. **Status timeout values.** How long should `Start` and `supervise` wait for a ready driver before failing? The backends wait 30s on Docker and 1m on Lambda, measured from the platform reporting the sandbox running, so the image entrypoint’s time counts against it. Should the budget be split (platform boot, entrypoint, driver answering), or made a workspace setting for images with slow entrypoints?
9. **Idle-timeout limits.** Should the runner cap `idle_timeout` (warm sandboxes hold host memory or account quota outside the concurrency semaphore), and should warm sandboxes count toward any limit?
10. **Runner crash during `Create`.** The runner records the handle as soon as `Create` returns, so only a runner that dies inside `Create` (during the platform call, or during a create-and-boot on a platform with no identity before boot) or between `Create` returning and the record write leaves a sandbox the platform created with no record, as does a `Create` whose cleanup after a failed provisioning step fails. Should `Prune` find such sandboxes by the gritz labels or tags the backend sets on create and destroy those with no taskstate record?
11. **Runner key rotation.** Sandboxes hold the public key they were created with. Should a runner that rotates its key re-deliver the new one through the backend’s channel, or keep old keys around until those sandboxes are destroyed?
12. **Half-open streams.** The driver releases a stream only when a write to it fails. A proxy that accepts writes for a client that is already gone would keep the old stream “open” and make every new `Run` return `Unavailable`. Should streams also have a maximum lifetime, or should a new `Run` from the same runner replace the old stream instead of being rejected? On the runner side, the driver client already cancels a `Run` stream that receives nothing for 45s (`driverclient.ErrStreamIdle`), so a half-open stream does not block the runner; only the driver’s side is open.

# End-to-end tests on a local backend

> No test runs the server, runner and driver together; existing tests stop at RPC handlers or use in-memory stand-ins, so cross-component bugs go uncaught.

Issue: <https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/issues/1890> (related)

## Problem

[Section titled “Problem”](#problem)

No test runs the server, the runner and the driver together. The apiserver tests (`internal/server/apiserver/*_test.go`) use a real Postgres store but stop at the RPC handlers. The runner tests (`internal/runner/*_test.go`) run a real `TaskManager`, but against `testrunner.Server`, an in-memory stand-in for `ListRunnerEvents`, and a `gritzclient.ClientMock` that accepts every runner event and reports every task `COMPLETED`. Their sandboxes come from `backend/fake`, and the drivers are either real `driverserver`s served in-process by `testrunner.NewDriver` (with their own `ClientMock`) or scripted stubs. The only test that uses a real backend, `TestTaskManagerStart`, needs a Docker daemon and still talks to a mocked server.

The bugs that matter live in the seams between those pieces. The run boundary in #1868 was a server bug that only showed up once the runner consumed the server’s command events. Neither side’s tests could see it, because each side tested against its own idea of the other. The runner-event-replica work (`proposals/implemented/runner-event-replica.md`) moves behaviour across those seams one slice at a time, and each slice has rebuilt the test plumbing to keep the existing tests passing. #1890 lists what that has left behind: `testrunner` grown piecemeal, polling helpers that only exist for intermediate designs, follower and `handled` tests that slices 8–9 make obsolete, and `driverserver` and fake backend tests reworked twice.

The many small runner tests are also hard to trust. They assert on `WaitHandled`, the outbox’s length, fake-backend counters (`Boots`, `Runs`) and `AssertTracked`’s probe `Boot`, which is the runner’s internal bookkeeping rather than what a user sees. When the runner’s design changes they all change with it, so they don’t tell us whether behaviour survived the change.

We want a few real end-to-end tests over many small, questionable ones. They should exercise the real server, runner and driver, use fakes only where there is no other way, and assert only what a user can observe. Then we want to port the existing tests onto them and delete what they cover.

## Design

[Section titled “Design”](#design)

```plaintext
 test ──RPCs (web UI / MCP)──▶ h.Server: apiserver (httptest, teststore Postgres)
                                 ▲   │ SSE notifications
          SubmitRunnerEvents,    │   ▼
          logs, MCP tools        │ h.Runner: runner.Serve (temp runner.db)
                                 │   │
                                 │   ▼ h.Backend: local backend
                               driver process (prebuilt gritz driver --prefix DIR)   black box
                                     │ Agent.Prompt
                                     ▼
                               puppet agent ──HTTP──▶ h.Agent: each Prompt call is a run the test holds open
```

Only two things are fake:

* **The sandbox** is a directory on the runner host, and the driver is an ordinary child process. The local backend provides it.
* **The agent** is a new `puppet` agent (below). It has no behaviour of its own: it forwards each `Prompt` call to the harness, and the test decides when and how the run ends.

Everything else is production code: the apiserver behind its real auth, the runner’s real wiring on its own SQLite `runner.db`, the prebuilt driver binary the Docker backend ships, the real driver.v1 transport over a Unix socket, the injected `gritz` MCP server, log shipping and secret masking.

**The driver is a black box.** It has no public API of its own: the runner and the API server configure it, and the harness has no handle on it and no mocks of it. Tests see it only through its effects:

* the files its setup commands write in the sandbox directory;
* the runs it gives the agent: each `Prompt` call, with its prompt, and whether it is cancelled;
* what it reports to the server: runner events with their versions, log chunks, and the events its tool calls create.

Tests interfere with it only from outside: its calls to the server through `h.Server.Mock`, and its sandbox through `h.Backend`, including `KillDriver`.

**Faults are injected at the seams, with moq mocks rather than hand-written fakes.** A mock installed on the server or the backend replaces the methods it sets, for every caller, until it is removed. Every other method reaches the real implementation.

### Local backend

[Section titled “Local backend”](#local-backend)

`internal/runner/backend/local` implements `backend.Backend` by using the runner host as the sandbox, with no isolation. It is for tests and development (`gritz runner --backend local`), never for running untrusted agents.

Each sandbox is a directory `Root/<task id>`. The handle is `backend.Handle{Type: "local", ID: "<task id>"}`, so the harness can find a task’s directory without reading the runner’s records. Naming by task id mirrors Docker’s `gritz-<task id>` container names.

| Operation           | Local backend                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Create`            | `mkdir Root/<id>` (fails if it exists, as a Docker name clash does). Nothing is copied: the driver binary is run in place.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `Boot`              | No-op if up; `ErrGone` if the directory is missing. Otherwise starts `Binary driver --addr unix://DIR/gritz/driver.sock --prefix DIR` as a child process and writes its pid to `DIR/gritz/driver.pid`. The process runs with working directory `DIR` and environment `Environ` plus `HOME=DIR/home`, in its own process group (`Setpgid`), with stdout and stderr appended to `DIR/gritz/driver.out`. Boot returns once the process has started; driver readiness stays the runner’s job, as with Docker. |
| `Dial`              | A driver client over the socket: unencrypted HTTP/2 with prior knowledge and the JWT as bearer, the same transport the Docker backend uses minus the exec tunnel.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `Suspend`           | `SIGTERM` to the driver, which stops its run and reports it, as `docker stop` does. Waits for it to exit, then `SIGKILL`s the process group after `suspendTimeout`. The directory stays, so the next `Boot` finds the driver’s files where it left them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `Destroy`           | `SIGKILL` the process group, then remove the directory. A missing directory is not an error.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `Kill` (local only) | `SIGKILL` the process group and leave the directory. Not part of `backend.Sandbox`; `h.Backend.KillDriver` uses it to produce a real lost run.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `Status`            | `gone` if the directory is missing; `up` if the pid file names a live process whose `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` carries `--prefix DIR`; `suspended` otherwise.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `Open`              | Rehydrates from the handle, with no I/O.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `Close`             | Does nothing. Drivers outlive the backend, as containers outlive a Docker client.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `ValidateWorkspace` | Accepts every workspace. The local backend reads no runtime section (`container:`, `lambda_microvm:`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Who reaps the driver.** `Boot` starts a goroutine that `Wait`s for the process and then removes the pid file. That goroutine belongs to the OS process, not to the `Backend` value, so after `h.Runner.Restart()` the old backend’s goroutine still reaps a driver that a new backend instance in the same test process suspends. A zombie therefore never looks up. In development, a restarted `gritz runner` process leaves its drivers to `init`. They are in their own process group, so a Ctrl-C to the runner doesn’t reach them, and the new runner finds them through the pid file.

**Socket path length.** A Unix socket path is limited to 107 bytes, and `t.TempDir()` paths with long test names exceed that. `New` rejects a `Root` whose longest socket path would be too long, and the harness puts its root under `os.MkdirTemp("", "gritz-e2e-")` rather than `t.TempDir()`.

**The injected MCP server’s binary.** The runner points the injected `gritz` MCP server at `backend.BinaryPath` (`/usr/local/bin/gritz`), which is where Docker copies the binary and where the Lambda image has it (`TaskManager.spec`). On the local backend the binary is wherever `Options.Binary` says. A new method on `backend.Backend` lets every backend say where; Docker and Lambda return `backend.BinaryPath`:

```go
// BinaryPath returns the path of the gritz binary inside the backend's
// sandboxes, which the injected MCP server runs.
BinaryPath() string
```

`TaskManager.spec` uses it for `McpServer.Command`.

### Per-sandbox driver paths

[Section titled “Per-sandbox driver paths”](#per-sandbox-driver-paths)

Every path the driver and the agent use must sit inside the sandbox directory so that parallel sandboxes on one host don’t collide. Here is what the driver and agent touch today, and what makes each per sandbox:

| Path                                                                                                         | Defined by                                                                          | How it becomes per sandbox                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/gritz/run.json`                                                                                            | `runrecord.Path`                                                                    | `PrefixPath` (below)                                                                                |
| `/gritz/events.jsonl`                                                                                        | `eventfile.Path`                                                                    | `PrefixPath`                                                                                        |
| `/gritz/log`                                                                                                 | `agent.DefaultLogPath`                                                              | `PrefixPath`                                                                                        |
| `/tmp/gritz/<id>.json`, the agent config store                                                               | `agent.DefaultConfigStore`                                                          | `PrefixPath`                                                                                        |
| `RunSpec.files` (the config store directory and file, the `/gritz` directory) and `/gritz/.provisioned`      | `TaskManager.spec`, `driverserver.ProvisionedPath`                                  | `PrefixPath` (today `FileRoot`)                                                                     |
| `/gritz/driver.sock`                                                                                         | `docker.DriverAddr`                                                                 | `--addr`, already a flag                                                                            |
| `/usr/local/bin/gritz` in the agent config                                                                   | `backend.BinaryPath`                                                                | `Backend.BinaryPath()` (above)                                                                      |
| `$HOME` (the agent CLIs’ `os.UserHomeDir()` in `codex.go`, `cursor.go`, `sloppy.go`; `claude`’s `~/.claude`) | the process environment                                                             | the local backend sets `HOME=DIR/home` on the driver, and runs inherit it through `Options.Environ` |
| The agent’s and setup commands’ working directory                                                            | `agent.Config.Cwd`, defaulting to `.` (`interface.go`); setup commands set no `Dir` | the driver’s working directory, which the local backend sets to `DIR`                               |
| `/gritz/driver.pid`, `/gritz/driver.out`                                                                     | new, local backend only                                                             | inside `DIR`                                                                                        |

Most of this already exists. `driverserver.Options` and `ExecutorOptions` have `RecordPath`, `EventsPath`, `LogPath`, `Config` and `FileRoot`, but only the tests set them (`testrunner.NewDriver` and `driverserver_test.go`’s `setup`), and they build the same layout by hand. These five options are replaced by one:

```go
// PrefixPath is prepended to every in-sandbox path: the run record, the event
// file, the driver log, the agent config store, the RunSpec files and the
// provisioned marker. Defaults to "/".
PrefixPath string
```

`gritz driver` gains `--prefix` to set it. It is only a path prefix, not a chroot: nothing is isolated. A sandbox’s paths are its in-container paths under `PrefixPath`, so the runner keeps sending absolute paths in `RunSpec.files` and needs no change. Docker and Lambda keep the default `/`.

### The puppet agent

[Section titled “The puppet agent”](#the-puppet-agent)

The test needs per-run control of what the agent does: keep run 1 going until the test has cancelled it, let run 2 finish, make run 3 fail. Doing that with scripts (a fenced block in the instructions that the dummy agent parses and runs) or with timed sleeps makes scenarios depend on timing and on a script format, and the dummy’s workspace-level `DummyOptions` can’t vary per run at all.

Instead, a new agent type, **`puppet`**, has no behaviour of its own. It forwards each `Agent.Prompt` call to the harness, and the test answers it. It lives in its own package, `internal/runner/agent/puppet`, which holds both sides: the client `puppet.Agent` the driver runs, and the `puppet.Server` the harness serves. The package doesn’t import `agent`; `agent.NewAgent` builds a `puppet.Agent` for `TypePuppet`, and `agent.Config` holds `*puppet.Options`.

* **One HTTP request per `Prompt`.** The workspace points the puppet at the harness (`agent: puppet: url: …`). Under the local backend the driver runs on the runner host, so it can reach an `httptest` endpoint in the test process. `Prompt(ctx, prompt, resume)` posts `{task_id, prompt, resume}`, with the task id from `GRITZ_TASK_ID`, and holds the request open until the harness replies with success or an error message. `Prompt` returns nil or that error.
