Verifiable by: building an image with the example script, checking that its output shows up in `/aws/lambda-microvms/<image-name>`, and comparing cold MCP start time on a VM launched from it.

## Trade-offs

[Section titled “Trade-offs”](#trade-offs)

* **A flag (chosen) vs. a fixed path under `/gritz/`.** A fixed `/gritz/validate` would put image content in a directory that gritz creates and writes to at runtime, and the permissions conflict:

  * Docker backend: the runner creates `/gritz` as a `0777` directory when it creates the container, so that a non-root driver can write `driver.sock`, `run.json` and `log` (`internal/runner/backend/docker/docker.go`, `internal/runner/taskmanager.go`). A `COPY validate /gritz/validate` in the image would create `/gritz` as root-owned `0755` instead.
  * Lambda backend: the driver creates `/gritz/*` itself (`provision` and `writeFile` in `internal/runner/driverserver/driverserver.go`). If the image creates `/gritz` as root-owned `0755` and the driver isn’t root, the driver can’t write `run.json`, `log` or `.provisioned`.

  With the flag, the author picks the path in the `ENTRYPOINT` they already write, and gritz claims no location in the image. The flag also makes the intent explicit, so a wrong path can fail the build at startup instead of quietly turning off prefetching.

* **Commands in workspace config:** rejected. The image is built with `create-microvm-image`, outside any workspace. One image can serve several workspaces, and the runner is not involved in the build.

* **Blocking until the script exits:** simpler, but AWS explicitly says not to hold hook requests open, and a request still open when the timeout runs out ends the build. Returning 503 while the script runs is the documented contract.

* **Warming in `/ready`, before the snapshot:** the page cache would be in the memory snapshot. But Lambda only tracks prefetch regions during validation, and processes started before the snapshot would be frozen into every VM. `/validate` is the hook meant for this.

* **Ignoring script failures:** warmup could never fail the build, but that throws away the only cheap build-time check that the image works. `|| true` gives authors control per command.

* **A timeout in the driver:** rejected. `validateTimeoutInSeconds` already limits the build, and when it runs out Lambda discards the VM.

## Open Questions

[Section titled “Open Questions”](#open-questions)

* Does the validate MicroVM have the build’s network egress? The script shouldn’t need the network to read files that are already in the image, but some tools phone home on start (update checks). Without egress, those tools may hang until their own timeouts and use up the validate time limit.
* Is 900s a good README default for `validateTimeoutInSeconds`, or should the example use the 3600s maximum, since a build that times out just has to be re-run?

# Link Routing URL

> Event routing needs exact URL string equality, so webhooks collapse events to the parent resource URL and links must match byte-for-byte.

Issue: <https://github.com/icholy/gritz/issues/810>

## Problem

[Section titled “Problem”](#problem)

Event routing matches events to tasks by **exact string equality** on a URL. `FindSubscribedLinksForOrgs` (`internal/store/sql/queries/link.sql`) runs `WHERE l.url = $1 ...`, and `eventrouter.Router.Route` feeds it `input.URL` verbatim. So the URL an agent stores on a link must be byte-identical to the URL a future webhook produces.

To make that hold, the webhook handlers deliberately collapse every event to its *parent* resource URL (`internal/server/githubserver/webhook.go`):

| Event                         | URL stored today                                          |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `issue_comment`               | `event.Issue.HTMLURL` (the issue/PR, **not** the comment) |
| `pull_request_review_comment` | `event.PullRequest.HTMLURL` (the PR, **not** the comment) |
| `pull_request_review`         | `event.PullRequest.HTMLURL` (the PR, **not** the review)  |

An event triggered by a specific comment therefore links to the whole issue, and the agent has to be steered toward the one URL form that will match. In practice agents also store **API URLs** (e.g. `api.github.com/repos/o/r/issues/5`) because that is what the JSON responses from GitHub/Jira MCP servers return, and those never match the web URLs the webhooks produce.

The issue proposes giving links (and events) **two URLs**: the original expressive `url`, and a `routing_url` derived from it that is used solely for routing.

## Design

[Section titled “Design”](#design)

### Core idea

[Section titled “Core idea”](#core-idea)

Add a `routing_url` column to `task_links`, derived from `url` by `model.RoutingURL`. Routing matches on the link’s `routing_url` instead of its `url`. `url` stays expressive and user-facing; `routing_url` is an internal key.

The `events` table does **not** get a `routing_url` column. Routing matches on the *link* side, and nothing queries events by URL (the only such query, `FindEventsByURL`, is removed — see Cleanup). The router still derives a routing key to look up links, but it doesn’t need to persist that key on the event; the event keeps its expressive `url` for display.

`RoutingURL` only normalizes URLs it recognizes (GitHub issue/PR and Jira issue, in both their **web and API** forms). Everything else is returned unchanged — there is no general-purpose normalization.

### 1. Routing URL derivation

[Section titled “1. Routing URL derivation”](#1-routing-url-derivation)

New code in `internal/model/url.go` (which already houses `TaskURL`):

```go
// RoutingURL reduces a recognized resource URL to a stable routing key, so two
// URLs that point at the same logical resource — a comment vs. its issue, or an
// API URL vs. its web URL — produce the same key. Only recognized URLs are
// normalized; anything else is returned unchanged.
//
//   github.com/o/r/issues/5#issuecomment-9            -> github.com/o/r/issues/5
//   github.com/o/r/pull/5/files                       -> github.com/o/r/pull/5
//   api.github.com/repos/o/r/issues/5                 -> github.com/o/r/issues/5
//   api.github.com/repos/o/r/pulls/5                  -> github.com/o/r/pull/5
//   site.atlassian.net/browse/X-1?focusedCommentId=2  -> site.atlassian.net/browse/X-1
//   site.atlassian.net/rest/api/2/issue/X-1           -> site.atlassian.net/browse/X-1
func RoutingURL(raw string) string
```

GitHub, web host `github.com`: path `/{owner}/{repo}/{issues|pull}/{n}[/...]` → `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/{kind}/{n}`. Collapses `#issuecomment-…`, `#discussion_r…`, `#pullrequestreview-…`, `/files`, `/commits/…`. Issues and pull requests stay distinct (`/issues/5` ≠ `/pull/5`).

GitHub, API host `api.github.com`: path `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/{issues|pulls}/{n}` → the same web key (`issues`→`/issues/`, `pulls`→`/pull/`). API comment URLs that don’t embed the parent number (`/repos/o/r/issues/comments/{id}`) can’t be reduced and are returned unchanged — noted as a limitation.

Jira, web `/browse/{KEY}[?…]` → `https://{host}/browse/{KEY}`; API `/rest/api/{v}/issue/{KEY}` → `https://{host}/browse/{KEY}` (mirrors the existing `Issue.BrowseURL` logic in `internal/x/atlassian/webhook.go`). API URLs that use a numeric issue id rather than the key can’t be mapped without a lookup and are returned unchanged.

Anything else: returned unchanged (matches by exact equality, as today).

`RoutingURL` gets a thorough unit test table covering each web/API/comment/fragment form plus non-matching hosts and malformed input.

### 2. Where `routing_url` is set

[Section titled “2. Where routing_url is set”](#2-where-routing_url-is-set)

`routing_url` is **derived in the application/RPC layer, not in the store** — deriving it is domain logic, and the store should only persist what it is handed. So `store.CreateLink` / `store.CreateEvent` simply write the `RoutingURL` field as given.

* **`gritz:create_link` (apiserver).** `Server.CreateLink` (`internal/server/apiserver/link.go`) sets the field when it builds the model:

  ```go
  link := &model.Link{
      TaskID:     req.TaskId,
      Relevance:  req.Relevance,
      URL:        req.Url,
      RoutingURL: model.RoutingURL(req.Url),
      Title:      req.Title,
      Subscribe:  req.Subscribe,
      CreatedAt:  time.Now(),
  }
  ```

* **Event routing (`eventrouter`).** The router already computes the routing key (see §3) and sets it on the auto-created subscribed link before calling the store.

`CreateLinkRequest` itself is unchanged — clients still send only `url`; the server derives `routing_url`.

### 3. `InputEvent.RoutingURL` and the Router

[Section titled “3. InputEvent.RoutingURL and the Router”](#3-inputeventroutingurl-and-the-router)

Add a `RoutingURL string` field to `eventrouter.InputEvent`. The webhook handlers populate it directly — they usually **already have** the parent issue/PR URL on hand, so no parsing is needed:

```go
type InputEvent struct {
    // ... existing fields ...
    URL        string // expressive: the comment/review that triggered the event
    RoutingURL string // routing key; webhooks set this from the parent they already have
}
```

`Router.Route` uses `RoutingURL` when the producer supplied it, and only falls back to deriving from `URL` otherwise:

```go
key := input.RoutingURL
if key == "" {
    key = model.RoutingURL(input.URL)
}
linksByOrg, err := r.links(ctx, key, orgIDs)   // FindSubscribedLinksForOrgs(key, ...)
...
event := &model.Event{
    Description: input.Description,
    Data:        input.Data,
    URL:         input.URL,   // the comment/review that triggered it
    OrgID:       orgID,
}
```

`key` is only used to look up links; it is not stored on the event (the `events` table has no `routing_url` column). The auto-created subscribed link in `Router.create`, however, is given the same `key` as its `RoutingURL`.

### 4. Webhook handlers — link to the real trigger

[Section titled “4. Webhook handlers — link to the real trigger”](#4-webhook-handlers--link-to-the-real-trigger)

The handlers set `URL` to the actual comment/review and `RoutingURL` to the parent they already extract (`internal/server/githubserver/webhook.go`):

| Event                            | `InputEvent.URL`        | `InputEvent.RoutingURL`     |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `issue_comment`                  | `event.Comment.HTMLURL` | `event.Issue.HTMLURL`       |
| `pull_request_review_comment`    | `event.Comment.HTMLURL` | `event.PullRequest.HTMLURL` |
| `pull_request_review`            | `event.Review.HTMLURL`  | `event.PullRequest.HTMLURL` |
| `issues`/`pull_request` assigned | parent URL (no comment) | same parent URL             |

These webhook URLs are already canonical, so the handlers can set `RoutingURL` without calling `model.RoutingURL` at all — matching the reviewer’s point that webhooks usually already have the routing URL.

Atlassian (`internal/server/atlassianserver/webhook.go`): set `URL` to the comment-focused browse URL when available, and `RoutingURL` to the plain issue browse URL it already builds via `Issue.BrowseURL()`.

### 5. Schema, model, proto

[Section titled “5. Schema, model, proto”](#5-schema-model-proto)

Migration `internal/store/sql/migrations/<ts>_link_routing_url.sql`:

```sql
-- migrate:up
ALTER TABLE task_links ADD COLUMN routing_url TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';


-- Existing rows already stored the canonical parent URL (the old contract),
-- so seeding routing_url = url preserves all current matches.
UPDATE task_links SET routing_url = url WHERE routing_url = '';


CREATE INDEX idx_task_links_routing_url ON task_links (routing_url);


-- migrate:down
DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_task_links_routing_url;
ALTER TABLE task_links DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS routing_url;
```

Only `task_links` gets the column. The existing `idx_task_links_url` / `idx_events_url` indexes are dropped, because their only users (`FindLinksByURL` / `FindEventsByURL`) are removed — see Cleanup below.

### 6. Cleanup: remove unused `FindLinksByURL` / `FindEventsByURL`

[Section titled “6. Cleanup: remove unused FindLinksByURL / FindEventsByURL”](#6-cleanup-remove-unused-findlinksbyurl--findeventsbyurl)

Both lookups are dead code today and routing no longer needs them, so they are removed rather than carried forward:

* **`FindEventsByURL`** (`store.FindEventsByURL` + the `event.sql` query) has no callers at all — no RPC, no CLI, no test.
* **`FindLinksByURL`** has a store method, an `event`/`link.sql` query, an RPC (`FindLinksByURLRequest`/`Response` + the `apiserver` handler), and generated stubs — but nothing consumes the RPC (not the webui, the CLI, the n8n node, nor the `gritzclient` wrapper). Removing it also drops the `FindLinksByURL` RPC from `proto/gritz/v1/gritz.proto`.

This leaves `FindSubscribedLinksForOrgs` (now matching on `routing_url`) as the only URL-based lookup, and removes the `idx_task_links_url` / `idx_events_url` indexes that backed the deleted queries.

Queries: `CreateLink` inserts `routing_url`; the link `SELECT`s return it; `FindSubscribedLinksForOrgs` matches `WHERE l.routing_url = sqlc.arg(routing_url)`. The `events` queries are unchanged (no `routing_url`). `model.Link` gains a `RoutingURL string` field (with `Proto` / `FromProto` wiring); `model.Event` is unchanged. Proto adds a read-only `string routing_url` to `TaskLink` (field 8) only.

## Trade-offs

[Section titled “Trade-offs”](#trade-offs)

* **Derive in the RPC/router layer vs. in the store.** Deriving `routing_url` is domain logic, so it lives with the callers that own the URL (the `CreateLink` RPC handler and the router) rather than in the persistence layer. The store stays a dumb writer. The cost is that each create path must set the field; there are only two.
* **Stored column vs. derive-at-query-time.** Storing `routing_url` keeps matching a single indexed equality lookup; the host-aware Go logic can’t be expressed as a Postgres index expression. The cost is a derived column that must be re-derived if the function changes (see Open Questions).
* **Webhook-supplied routing URL vs. always deriving.** The webhooks already carry the parent URL, so they set `RoutingURL` directly and the router skips derivation for events. `model.RoutingURL` is still the fallback (and the path for agent-created links, which is where API URLs show up).
* **Backward compatibility.** Existing rows are backfilled with `routing_url = url`. Because the old contract already required canonical parent URLs, those rows keep matching new events without a Go-side backfill.

## Open Questions

[Section titled “Open Questions”](#open-questions)

1. **Re-derivation on logic change.** If `RoutingURL` evolves, stored keys can drift. A one-shot backfill command can re-derive existing rows; acceptable to defer.
2. **Unmappable API URLs.** GitHub API comment URLs without the parent number, and Jira API URLs that use a numeric issue id, can’t be reduced to the web key without a network lookup. Proposed: leave them unchanged (they simply won’t cross-match a web URL). Worth confirming this is acceptable or whether a lookup is warranted.

# MCP admin tools and fuller task management

> The user-facing MCP only creates, lists, reads, updates and archives tasks, so events, custom event types, schedules and org data, plus several task operations the API and Web UI offer, can't be reached from an MCP client.

Issue: <https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/issues/2095>

## Problem

[Section titled “Problem”](#problem)

The user-facing MCP, served as `gritz mcp` over stdio and as `/mcp` on the server, registers six tools in [`internal/server/mcpserver`](https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/blob/master/internal/server/mcpserver/mcpserver.go): `list_workspaces`, `create_task`, `get_task`, `list_tasks`, `update_task` and `archive_task`. Everything else the `GritzService` API offers is unreachable from an MCP client, so an agent that a user works with locally can’t:

* **Administer events.** List the org’s external events, inspect or delete one, see which event types exist, define custom event types, dry-run an event against the routing rules, or send a custom event.
* **Manage schedules.** Create, edit, pause, delete or run one now.
* **Read org administration data or edit routing rules.** Who the members are, what API keys exist and when they expire, the org’s webhook and MCP URLs; the routing rules can’t be read or changed either.
* **Manage tasks fully.** Even the task tools lag the API and Web UI: there is no cancel, restart or unarchive, no rename, no paging past the 50 newest tasks, no archived tasks, no drafts or namespaces, and no access to the agent’s transcript.

The in-sandbox agent MCP (`gritz tool agent-mcp`, [`internal/runner/agentmcp`](https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/tree/master/internal/runner/agentmcp)) is out of scope. It serves a task’s own agent with a task token, and nothing here changes it.

## Design

[Section titled “Design”](#design)

Add tools to `mcpserver.AddTools`, every one a thin proxy over a `GritzService` RPC. Every capability below already has an RPC, because the Web UI uses it, so no RPCs, store changes or migrations are needed.

### Principles

[Section titled “Principles”](#principles)

* **One tool, one intent.** A tool maps onto one RPC, or onto a short fixed sequence where the RPC’s shape doesn’t fit an agent (read-modify-write for the replace-whole-set RPCs, a follow-up `GetTask` to return the changed task, as `update_task` and `archive_task` already do).
* **The API is the authority.** The tools check no permissions themselves. Each RPC already checks `caller.Scopes` (`authscope.OpEventWrite`, `OpOrgRead`, `OpKeyRead`, …) and owner-only rules, and the MCP caller is an ordinary API caller (an OAuth app JWT or an API key, both `authscope.Admin()` today). A denied call surfaces as an `mcpx.ErrorResult`, as now.
* **Org data is read-only, except routing rules.** No tool calls `AddOrgMember`, `RemoveOrgMember`, `CreateKey`, `DeleteKey`, `CreateOrg`, `DeleteOrg`, `GenerateAtlassianWebhookSecret`, `LinkGitHubInstallation`, or the account unlink RPCs. Those stay in the Web UI and CLI. Routing rules are the one org setting an agent writes, through `set_routing_rules`, because configuring routing is the admin work an agent is most often asked to do.
* **No secrets in results.** `GetOrgSettingsResponse.atlassian_webhook_secret` is dropped from `get_org_settings`. `ListKeys` returns only key metadata, never a token, so `list_keys` is safe as is.
* **Annotations tell the client what a tool does.** Reads set `ReadOnlyHint`; `delete_event`, `delete_schedule`, `delete_custom_event_type` and `set_routing_rules` set `DestructiveHint`, so clients that confirm destructive calls do.
* **Same tools on both transports.** `gritz mcp` and `/mcp` share `AddTools`; every tool goes through the `gritzv1connect.GritzServiceHandler` interface, so none needs anything the Connect client can’t do.

### Task tools: audit and gaps

[Section titled “Task tools: audit and gaps”](#task-tools-audit-and-gaps)

What the API and Web UI do with tasks, against the MCP today:

| Capability                      | RPC                                                 | Web UI                               | MCP today                         | Proposal                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| List, paged, with archived      | `ListTasks` (`page_size`, `page_token`, `archived`) | yes                                  | first page of 50, unarchived only | `list_tasks` takes `page_size`, `page_token`, `archived`; returns `next_page_token`                                        |
| Task fields in lists            | `Task`                                              | status, archived badge, auto-archive | id, name, workspace, status, url  | summary adds `runner`, `namespace`, `archived`, `created_at`, `updated_at`                                                 |
| Read task + timeline            | `GetTask`, `ListEventsByTask`, `ListLinks`          | yes                                  | yes, every event                  | `get_task` adds `auto_archive`, `archived`, `namespace`, `actions`, timestamps; takes `event_types` to filter the timeline |
| Create as draft, in a namespace | `CreateTask` (`draft`, `namespace`)                 | yes (always draft)                   | no                                | `create_task` takes `draft`, `namespace`                                                                                   |
| Rename                          | `UpdateTask.name`                                   | no                                   | no                                | `update_task` takes `name`                                                                                                 |
| Change auto-archive             | `UpdateTask.auto_archive`                           | yes                                  | no                                | `update_task` takes `auto_archive`                                                                                         |
| Add instruction, start          | `UpdateTask`                                        | yes                                  | yes                               | `instruction` becomes optional, so a call can only rename or start                                                         |
| Cancel                          | `CancelTask`                                        | yes                                  | no                                | `cancel_task`                                                                                                              |
| Restart                         | `RestartTask`                                       | yes                                  | no                                | `restart_task`                                                                                                             |
| Archive                         | `ArchiveTask`                                       | yes                                  | yes                               | unchanged                                                                                                                  |
| Unarchive                       | `UnarchiveTask`                                     | yes                                  | no                                | `unarchive_task`                                                                                                           |
| Agent transcript                | `ListLogChunksByTask`                               | yes (Logs tab)                       | no                                | `get_task_log`                                                                                                             |
| Link a resource                 | `CreateLink`                                        | no                                   | no                                | `create_link`                                                                                                              |
| Shell                           | `OpenShell`                                         | yes                                  | no                                | out of scope: an interactive terminal, not a tool call                                                                     |

`get_task` returning `actions` (`TaskActions`: archive, cancel, restart, start, unarchive) lets the agent see what the task allows before it tries, the same flags the Web UI uses to enable its buttons.

### Tool set

[Section titled “Tool set”](#tool-set)

Existing tools are marked *(changed)* or *(unchanged)*; the rest are new.

#### Tasks

[Section titled “Tasks”](#tasks)

| Tool                            | RPC                                        | Arguments                                                                          |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_workspaces` *(unchanged)* | `ListWorkspaces`                           | —                                                                                  |
| `list_tasks` *(changed)*        | `ListTasks`                                | `page_size`, `page_token`, `archived`                                              |
| `get_task` *(changed)*          | `GetTask`, `ListEventsByTask`, `ListLinks` | `id`, `event_types`                                                                |
| `create_task` *(changed)*       | `CreateTask`                               | `workspace`, `runner`, `instruction`, `name`, `auto_archive`, `namespace`, `draft` |
| `update_task` *(changed)*       | `UpdateTask`, `GetTask`                    | `id`, `instruction`, `url`, `name`, `auto_archive`, `start`                        |
| `cancel_task`                   | `CancelTask`, `GetTask`                    | `id`                                                                               |
| `restart_task`                  | `RestartTask`, `GetTask`                   | `id`                                                                               |
| `archive_task` *(unchanged)*    | `ArchiveTask`, `GetTask`                   | `id`                                                                               |
| `unarchive_task`                | `UnarchiveTask`, `GetTask`                 | `id`                                                                               |
| `get_task_log`                  | `ListLogChunksByTask`                      | `id`, `before`, `max_bytes`                                                        |
| `create_link`                   | `CreateLink`                               | `task_id`, `url`, `title`, `relevance`, `subscribe`                                |

Details:

* **`list_tasks`** returns `{tasks, next_page_token}` instead of a bare array. `page_size` defaults to the server’s 50.
* **`get_task`**’s `event_types` is passed to `gritzclient.ListAllEventsByTask`, which already sends it as `ListEventsByTaskRequest.types` (the tool passes `nil` today), so an agent that only wants the instructions or the external events doesn’t page in the whole timeline. Empty means every type, as now; command events stay skipped.
* **`update_task`** rejects a call that sets none of `instruction`, `name`, `auto_archive` or `start` with an error result. `auto_archive` takes the Go duration strings `create_task` already parses; an unset argument leaves `UpdateTaskRequest.auto_archive` nil (leave alone).
* **`create_task`** with `draft: true` creates the task in `DRAFT`; the agent starts it later with `update_task` and `start: true`, the same flow as the Web UI’s composer. `instruction` stays required for a non-draft create.
* **`get_task_log`** returns the tail of the task’s transcript as text: it walks `ListLogChunksByTask` backwards from the newest page (empty `page_token`, then `prev_page_token`) until it has `max_bytes` (default 64 KiB, capped at 1 MiB) or history runs out, and returns `{log, before}`, where `before` is the `prev_page_token` to pass back for the preceding bytes, empty at the start of the log. Chunks are the shipped log, so declared secrets are already masked. The tool doesn’t parse the driver’s log format.
* **`create_link`** lets the user subscribe a task to a resource they made by hand, such as a PR opened outside gritz, so the task receives its events. It maps 1:1 onto `CreateLink`; `relevance` is free text describing why the link matters, as in the agent’s own `create_link`.

#### Events

[Section titled “Events”](#events)

| Tool           | RPC                  | Arguments                                                                  |
| -------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_events`  | `ListExternalEvents` | `limit`                                                                    |
| `get_event`    | `GetEvent`           | `id`                                                                       |
| `delete_event` | `DeleteEvent`        | `id`                                                                       |
| `test_event`   | `TestEvent`          | `source`, `type`, `body`, `url`, `attrs`, `description`, `details`, `fire` |

* **`list_events`** returns a summary per event: `id`, `task_id`, `source`, `type`, `description`, `url`, `created_at` from `ExternalPayload`, not the `data` blob. `get_event` returns the full event as protojson, like `get_task`’s timeline.
* **`test_event`** is for testing routing. It takes any registered source and type, defaults to a dry run (`fire: false`), and returns `TestEventResponse.matches`: which rule matched and whether it would wake or create. `fire: true` routes it for real; the RPC already requires `OpOrgWrite` for that. The RPC validates the event against its type and routes a custom event with no actor, exactly as `/webhook/custom` does, so firing a custom event is how an agent sends one; an invalid event comes back as an error result carrying the validation message.

#### Event types

[Section titled “Event types”](#event-types)

| Tool                       | RPC                                          | Arguments                |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `list_event_types`         | `GetEventTypes`                              | —                        |
| `put_custom_event_type`    | `GetCustomEventTypes`, `SetCustomEventTypes` | `type`, `label`, `attrs` |
| `delete_custom_event_type` | `GetCustomEventTypes`, `SetCustomEventTypes` | `type`                   |

* **`list_event_types`** lists the built-in and custom types with their attributes, which is what an agent needs to fill in `test_event`’s attrs, or to write a routing rule’s conditions.
* `SetCustomEventTypes` replaces the whole set. The two write tools read the current set, add, replace or remove the one entry by `type`, and write the set back, exactly as the Web UI’s custom event type pages do. The RPC validates the result: a malformed schema is `InvalidArgument`, and removing a type a routing rule still uses is `FailedPrecondition`, which the tool returns as an error result naming the problem. `source` is always `"custom"` and is not an argument.

#### Schedules

[Section titled “Schedules”](#schedules)

| Tool                   | RPC                             | Arguments                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list_schedules`       | `ListSchedules`                 | —                                                                                                             |
| `get_schedule`         | `GetSchedule`                   | `id`                                                                                                          |
| `create_schedule`      | `CreateSchedule`                | `name`, `workspace`, `runner`, `namespace`, `instruction`, `cron_expr`, `timezone`, `auto_archive`, `enabled` |
| `update_schedule`      | `GetSchedule`, `UpdateSchedule` | `id`, and any of the create arguments except `enabled`                                                        |
| `set_schedule_enabled` | `SetScheduleEnabled`            | `id`, `enabled`                                                                                               |
| `run_schedule`         | `RunSchedule`                   | `id`                                                                                                          |
| `delete_schedule`      | `DeleteSchedule`                | `id`                                                                                                          |

* Schedules take one `instruction`, like `create_task`, mapped to a one-element `instructions`. A schedule with several stored instructions is shown with all of them by `get_schedule`; `update_schedule` without `instruction` keeps them.
* `UpdateScheduleRequest` replaces every template field. `update_schedule` takes each as optional (pointer fields in the input struct), loads the schedule with `GetSchedule`, overlays the arguments given and sends the full request, so “change the cron to 9am” doesn’t blank the instructions.
* `create_schedule` defaults `enabled` to `false`, as the RPC does; the tool description says so, so an agent turns it on deliberately.
* `run_schedule` returns the created task’s summary.

#### Org

[Section titled “Org”](#org)

| Tool                | RPC               | Arguments |
| ------------------- | ----------------- | --------- |
| `list_members`      | `ListOrgMembers`  | —         |
| `list_keys`         | `ListKeys`        | —         |
| `get_org_settings`  | `GetOrgSettings`  | —         |
| `get_routing_rules` | `GetRoutingRules` | —         |
| `set_routing_rules` | `SetRoutingRules` | `rules`   |

* `list_members` returns `user_id`, `email`, `name`, `role`, `created_at`.
* `list_keys` returns `id`, `name`, `expires_at`, `created_at`.
* `get_org_settings` returns `mcp_url`, `custom_webhook_url`, `atlassian_webhook_url`, `github_app_url`, `github_installation_id`, and never `atlassian_webhook_secret`.
* `get_routing_rules` returns the rules as protojson.
* `set_routing_rules` proxies `SetRoutingRules` as is: `rules` is the full list as protojson `RoutingRule`s, in the shape `get_routing_rules` returns. The agent reads the list, edits it, and writes the whole list back. The tool description says that it replaces every rule in the org, so a list missing a rule deletes it. The RPC validates every rule against the org’s event types and returns `InvalidArgument` naming the bad rule, which the tool returns as an error result. It returns the stored rules.

### Instructions

[Section titled “Instructions”](#instructions)

`mcpserver.Instructions` grows a sentence saying the server also administers the org’s events, custom event types, schedules and routing rules, and reads its members and keys, so clients route those requests here.

### Code layout

[Section titled “Code layout”](#code-layout)

`mcpserver.go` holds the server, `AddTools` and the shared helpers (`taskSummary`, duration parsing). The handlers move into one file per domain, each with a `register` function `AddTools` calls in order:

```plaintext
internal/server/mcpserver/
  mcpserver.go   // NewServer, AddTools, Handler, Instructions, shared helpers
  task.go        // addTaskTools: task and workspace tools
  event.go       // addEventTools: events, event types, test and custom events
  schedule.go    // addScheduleTools
  org.go         // addOrgTools: members, keys, settings, routing rules
```

Tests stay on the existing pattern in `mcpserver_test.go`: a `gritzclient.ClientMock` behind an in-memory MCP session, asserting the RPC request each tool sends and the result it renders, plus `TestListTools` for the registered names. The test file splits along the same lines.

### API

[Section titled “API”](#api)

The package’s exported API doesn’t change: `AddTools` registers more tools.

```go
package mcpserver // github.com/gritzapp/gritz/internal/server/mcpserver


// Instructions is the prompt shown to MCP clients describing what the gritz server offers.
const Instructions = "..." // changed: mentions events, schedules, routing rules and org data


// AddTools registers the user-facing gritz tools on the given MCP server.
func AddTools(server *mcp.Server, service gritzv1connect.GritzServiceHandler, opts ...Option) // changed: registers the new tools
```

**How it fits:** unchanged. The server’s `/mcp` handler and `gritz mcp` both call `AddTools`; the server passes the in-process `apiserver.Server`, `gritz mcp` the Connect client. Every handler calls `GritzServiceHandler` methods only.

### Considered and left out

[Section titled “Considered and left out”](#considered-and-left-out)

* **Per-type custom event type RPCs** (`PutCustomEventType`, `DeleteCustomEventType`). They would remove the lost-update window of read-modify-write, but the Web UI has the same window and edits are rare.
* **Per-rule routing-rule RPCs.** Rules have no IDs, so per-rule add and remove would need stable rule IDs in `RoutingRule`. Proxying `SetRoutingRules` is what the Web UI’s rule editor does already.
* **`ListTasks` filters** (status, workspace, namespace). Useful to an agent hunting for “my failed tasks”, but the Web UI doesn’t filter either; paging covers it for now.
* **`ListExternalEvents` paging.** It returns at most the 100 newest events. That’s enough for an agent looking at recent activity, and the Web UI has the same limit.

## Implementation Plan

[Section titled “Implementation Plan”](#implementation-plan)

Each slice updates the **Tools** section of `integrations/mcp` for the tools it adds or changes, in the same PR.

1. **Split the package** — Delivers: `mcpserver.go` split into `task.go` with the existing handlers and the per-domain `register` structure; no behaviour change. Depends on: nothing. Verifiable by: the existing `mcpserver` tests pass unchanged.
2. **Task tools** — Delivers: `list_tasks` paging and `archived`, the wider task summary, `get_task`’s extra fields and `event_types` filter; `create_task` `draft` and `namespace`; `update_task` `name`, `auto_archive`, optional `instruction` and the nothing-to-do error; `cancel_task`, `restart_task`, `unarchive_task`; `get_task_log`; `create_link`. Depends on: (1). Verifiable by: mock tests on the requests each tool sends, including `next_page_token` in the `list_tasks` result, the `types` passed to `ListEventsByTask`, and `get_task_log` walking several `ListLogChunksByTask` pages backwards, stopping at `max_bytes` and returning the right `before`; a manual cancel and restart through `gritz mcp` against a local server.
3. **Events and event types** — Delivers: `list_events`, `get_event`, `delete_event`, `list_event_types`, `put_custom_event_type`, `delete_custom_event_type`, `test_event`. Updates `integrations/custom-events` to mention firing a custom event with `test_event`. Depends on: (1). Verifiable by: mock tests, including that `list_events` omits `data`, that the written custom type set adds, replaces or removes exactly one entry, that `test_event` sends `body`, `url` and multi-valued `attrs`, and that a `FailedPrecondition` or `InvalidArgument` comes back as an error result.
4. **Schedules** — Delivers: `list_schedules`, `get_schedule`, `create_schedule`, `update_schedule`, `set_schedule_enabled`, `run_schedule`, `delete_schedule`. Depends on: (1). Verifiable by: mock tests, including that `update_schedule` with only `cron_expr` sends the loaded instructions back unchanged.
5. **Org** — Delivers: `list_members`, `list_keys`, `get_org_settings`, `get_routing_rules`, `set_routing_rules`. Depends on: (1). Verifiable by: mock tests, including that `get_org_settings` drops the webhook secret, that `set_routing_rules` sends the list unchanged and carries `DestructiveHint`, and that an `InvalidArgument` comes back as an error result.
6. **Instructions** — Delivers: the updated `mcpserver.Instructions` and the intro of `integrations/mcp` describing the wider tool set. Depends on: (2)–(5). Verifiable by: reading the page; `TestListTools` lists every tool.

Slices 2–5 depend only on (1) and can land in any order.

## Trade-offs

[Section titled “Trade-offs”](#trade-offs)

* **Proxy tools over existing RPCs, not new MCP-specific endpoints.** Every capability already exists for the Web UI, with its authorization and validation. Proxying keeps `gritz mcp` and `/mcp` identical and keeps the MCP out of the permission model. The cost is a few read-modify-write tools where the RPC replaces a whole set.
* **Routing rules are written whole.** `set_routing_rules` proxies `SetRoutingRules`, which replaces the org’s whole rule list; one bad call from an agent that drops rules can silently stop events from waking tasks. Per-rule add and remove would be safer, but rules have no IDs to address them by. `DestructiveHint` and a description that says every rule is replaced make the client confirm, the RPC still validates every rule, and `get_routing_rules` plus `test_event` let the agent check its work.
* **A flat tool set, not toolsets.** The MCP goes from 6 tools to 30, which costs client context. Grouping tools behind a flag (`gritz mcp --tools task,event`) or MCP-level toolsets would trim it, but clients already let users disable individual tools, and the tool descriptions stay short. Revisit if it hurts.
* **`get_task_log` returns a byte tail, not parsed turns.** The transcript is the driver’s raw log in whatever format the agent CLI writes; parsing it per agent would couple the MCP to every agent integration. A byte budget keeps results bounded.
* **One instruction per create.** `CreateTask` and `CreateSchedule` accept several instructions, but nothing in the Web UI makes more than one, and one string is easier for an agent to fill.

# OAuth 2.1 for MCP endpoint

> The /mcp endpoint cannot be used as a Claude.ai custom connector because existing auth mechanisms are incompatible with the OAuth 2.1 authorization code flow with PKCE it requires.

Issue: <https://github.com/icholy/gritz/issues/417>

## Problem

[Section titled “Problem”](#problem)

The `/mcp` endpoint cannot be used as a Claude.ai custom connector because Claude.ai requires OAuth 2.1 authorization code flow with PKCE. The current auth mechanisms (API key with `X-Auth-Type` header, Zitadel Bearer tokens, cookie sessions) are not compatible with Claude.ai’s connector UI.

## Design

[Section titled “Design”](#design)

### Overview

[Section titled “Overview”](#overview)

Implement a minimal OAuth 2.1 authorization server within gritz. The user is already logged into the gritz web UI and has an app JWT (from `/auth/token`) scoped to their selected org. The authorize page sends this JWT to the backend, which verifies it and issues an auth code. No API keys or cookie auth involved in the OAuth flow.

### Sequence Diagram

[Section titled “Sequence Diagram”](#sequence-diagram)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User Browser
    participant C as Claude.ai
    participant X as gritz Server


    C->>X: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
    X->>C: authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, registration_endpoint


    C->>X: POST /oauth/register
    X->>C: client_id (generated UUID)


    C->>U: Open /ui/oauth/authorize?client_id&redirect_uri&code_challenge&state
    U->>X: GET /ui/oauth/authorize (SPA served, cookie auth)
    Note over U: User sees consent screen<br/>(identity + org from app JWT)
    U->>X: POST /oauth/authorize (app JWT + OAuth params)
    Note over X: Verify app JWT<br/>Sign auth code JWT (60s TTL)
    X->>U: Redirect to claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback?code&state
    U->>C: Auth code delivered


    C->>X: POST /oauth/token (code, client_id, code_verifier)
    Note over X: Verify auth code JWT<br/>Verify PKCE<br/>Sign new app JWT + refresh token
    X->>C: access_token, refresh_token, expires_in


    C->>X: MCP request (Authorization: Bearer <jwt>)
    X->>C: MCP response


    Note over C: Access token expires (5 min)
    C->>X: POST /oauth/token (grant_type=refresh_token, refresh_token)
    Note over X: Verify refresh token JWT<br/>Sign new app JWT + refresh token
    X->>C: access_token, refresh_token, expires_in
```

### New Routes

[Section titled “New Routes”](#new-routes)

| Method | Path                                      | Auth    | Description                               |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| GET    | `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | Public  | RFC 8414 metadata                         |
| GET    | `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`   | Public  | RFC 9728 resource metadata                |
| POST   | `/oauth/register`                         | Public  | Stub DCR – returns a generated client_id  |
| POST   | `/oauth/authorize`                        | App JWT | Verifies JWT, issues auth code, redirects |
| POST   | `/oauth/token`                            | Public  | Exchanges auth code for app JWT           |

The `GET /ui/oauth/authorize` page is handled by the React frontend. The backend only handles the `POST`.

### Discovery Metadata

[Section titled “Discovery Metadata”](#discovery-metadata)

`GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` returns:

```json
{
  "issuer": "https://gritz.example.com",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://gritz.example.com/ui/oauth/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://gritz.example.com/oauth/token",
  "response_types_supported": ["code"],
  "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"],
  "registration_endpoint": "https://gritz.example.com/oauth/register"
}
```

`GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` returns:

```json
{
  "resource": "https://gritz.example.com",
  "authorization_servers": ["https://gritz.example.com"]
}
```

### Registration Endpoint (Stub DCR)

[Section titled “Registration Endpoint (Stub DCR)”](#registration-endpoint-stub-dcr)

`POST /oauth/register` accepts a JSON body per [RFC 7591](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7591). The endpoint ignores most fields and returns a generated `client_id` (UUID) with no `client_secret`. This allows Claude.ai to automatically obtain a client_id without the user configuring one manually.

```json
// Request (most fields ignored)
{
  "client_name": "Claude",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback"]
}


// Response
{
  "client_id": "<generated-uuid>",
  "client_name": "Claude",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback"]
}
```

The client_id is not persisted – it’s only used for consistency checks between the authorize and token steps. Any valid UUID works.

### Authorization Endpoint

[Section titled “Authorization Endpoint”](#authorization-endpoint)

**Frontend (`/ui/oauth/authorize`)**: React page that reads the OAuth query params (`client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method`, `response_type`). Shows a consent screen with the user’s identity and org. On approve, POSTs the OAuth params plus the app JWT (from the existing auth context) to `/oauth/authorize`.

**Backend (`POST /oauth/authorize`)**: Verifies the app JWT from the request body via `VerifyAppToken()`. On success, signs an auth code JWT containing the user/org identity and OAuth params, then redirects to `redirect_uri?code=<code>&state=<state>`.

### Token Endpoint

[Section titled “Token Endpoint”](#token-endpoint)

`POST /oauth/token` accepts `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`:

| Parameter       | Description                                          |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `grant_type`    | Must be `authorization_code`                         |
| `code`          | The auth code from the authorize step                |
| `client_id`     | Must match the authorize request                     |
| `code_verifier` | PKCE verifier matching the original `code_challenge` |
| `redirect_uri`  | Must match the original `redirect_uri`               |

`client_secret` is accepted but ignored – PKCE is the sole proof of authorization.

**`grant_type=authorization_code`** validation:

1. Verify the auth code JWT signature and expiry
2. Verify `client_id` and `redirect_uri` match the JWT claims
3. Verify `code_verifier` against the JWT’s `code_challenge` (SHA256)

**`grant_type=refresh_token`** validation:

1. Verify the refresh token JWT signature and expiry

Both grant types return the same response shape. On success, sign a new app JWT and a new refresh token using `SignAppToken()` with the `UserInfo` from the auth code or refresh token:

```json
{
  "access_token": "<jwt>",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 300,
  "refresh_token": "<jwt>"
}
```

The refresh token is a signed JWT with the same user/org claims as the access token but with a longer TTL (30 days). Each refresh rotates the refresh token – a new one is issued every time. Refresh tokens cannot be revoked before expiry since there is no server-side state.

### Auth Code as Signed JWT

[Section titled “Auth Code as Signed JWT”](#auth-code-as-signed-jwt)

Auth codes are self-contained signed JWTs (60s TTL) containing all the state the token endpoint needs. This avoids shared state between server instances.

The auth code JWT uses the existing Ed25519 `AppKey` for signing:

```go
type authCodeClaims struct {
    jwt.RegisteredClaims
    // User identity from the app JWT
    Email         string `json:"email"`
    Name          string `json:"name"`
    OrgID         int64  `json:"org_id"`
    // OAuth params that must match at the token endpoint
    ClientID      string `json:"client_id"`
    RedirectURI   string `json:"redirect_uri"`
    CodeChallenge string `json:"code_challenge"`
}
```

The `POST /oauth/authorize` handler verifies the app JWT, extracts the user identity, and creates this auth code JWT. The `POST /oauth/token` handler verifies the signature, checks expiry, and validates the PKCE and OAuth params against the claims.

Since the code is signed and has a 60s TTL, replay is limited to the expiry window. Single-use enforcement is not possible without shared state, but the short TTL and PKCE `code_verifier` requirement make replay impractical.

No database migration needed. No shared state between instances.

### MCP Endpoint Auth Change

[Section titled “MCP Endpoint Auth Change”](#mcp-endpoint-auth-change)

The `/mcp` endpoint currently requires the `X-Auth-Type` header to determine auth strategy. Claude.ai sends a plain `Authorization: Bearer <token>` with no custom headers.

Modify the `RequireAuth` middleware’s default case (no `X-Auth-Type` header): after cookie auth fails, attempt app JWT validation via `VerifyAppToken()`. This allows the MCP endpoint to accept app JWTs issued by the OAuth token endpoint without any custom headers.

```go
// In RequireAuth, the default case (no X-Auth-Type header):
default:
    if !a.useDevUser(w, r, next) {
        // Try cookie auth first
        // If no cookie session, try app JWT from Bearer header
        // Fall back to cookie middleware (which will redirect to login)
    }
```

### New Package

[Section titled “New Package”](#new-package)

`internal/oauthflow/` containing:

* `oauthflow.go` – `Server` struct, `Options`, `New()` constructor
* `code.go` – auth code JWT claims, sign/verify helpers
* `handlers.go` – HTTP handlers for all 4 endpoints

The `Server` struct takes:

```go
type Options struct {
    AppKey  ed25519.PrivateKey
    BaseURL string
}
```

All dependencies are existing types. No new store queries or proto changes. `KeyValidator` is no longer needed.

### Route Registration in `server.go`

[Section titled “Route Registration in server.go”](#route-registration-in-servergo)

```go
oauthFlow := oauthflow.New(mcpauth.Options{
    AppKey:  appKey,
    BaseURL: s.baseURL,
})
mux.HandleFunc("/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server", oauthFlow.HandleMetadata)
mux.HandleFunc("/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", oauthFlow.HandleResourceMetadata)
mux.HandleFunc("/oauth/register", oauthFlow.HandleRegister)
mux.HandleFunc("/oauth/authorize", oauthFlow.HandleAuthorize)
mux.HandleFunc("/oauth/token", oauthFlow.HandleToken)
```

All routes are public – no auth middleware needed. The `/oauth/authorize` POST authenticates via the app JWT in the request body.

### Frontend Route

[Section titled “Frontend Route”](#frontend-route)

New React route at `webui/src/routes/oauth.authorize.tsx` (maps to `/ui/oauth/authorize`):

* Reads OAuth query params from the URL
* Shows the user’s identity and org (from the existing auth context)
* Has an “Approve” button that POSTs the OAuth params + app JWT to `/oauth/authorize`
* Shows error state if the POST fails

This page is behind cookie auth middleware (like all `/ui/` routes). The user must be logged in and have an org selected to have a valid app JWT.

### User Flow

[Section titled “User Flow”](#user-flow)

1. User adds a custom connector in Claude.ai with:

   * **URL**: `https://gritz.example.com/mcp`
   * **Client ID / Client Secret**: leave blank (Claude.ai auto-registers via DCR)

2. Claude.ai fetches discovery metadata, registers via `/oauth/register`, opens browser to `/ui/oauth/authorize`

3. If user is not logged into gritz, they log in via Zitadel (existing SSO flow)

4. User sees a consent screen showing their identity and org, clicks “Approve”

5. Frontend POSTs app JWT + OAuth params to `/oauth/authorize`

6. Backend verifies JWT, signs auth code JWT, redirects back to Claude.ai

7. Claude.ai exchanges the code at `/oauth/token` (PKCE verified) for a new app JWT

8. Claude.ai uses the JWT as Bearer token on `/mcp`

## Trade-offs

[Section titled “Trade-offs”](#trade-offs)

### Auth code as signed JWT vs. shared store

[Section titled “Auth code as signed JWT vs. shared store”](#auth-code-as-signed-jwt-vs-shared-store)

Auth codes are self-contained signed JWTs rather than random tokens looked up in a database or cache. This avoids shared state between server instances – any instance can verify the code using the shared `AppKey`. The tradeoff is that single-use enforcement is not possible (a code could theoretically be replayed within its 60s TTL), but PKCE makes this impractical since the attacker would also need the `code_verifier`.

### Stub DCR vs. persistent client registry

[Section titled “Stub DCR vs. persistent client registry”](#stub-dcr-vs-persistent-client-registry)

The `/oauth/register` endpoint generates a UUID but doesn’t persist it. The client_id is only checked for consistency between the authorize and token steps (it’s embedded in the auth code JWT). A persistent `oauth_clients` table would enable revocation, UI visibility of connected clients, and per-client configuration, but isn’t needed for the initial implementation.

### Refresh tokens are not revocable

[Section titled “Refresh tokens are not revocable”](#refresh-tokens-are-not-revocable)

Refresh tokens are signed JWTs with a 30-day TTL and no server-side state. They cannot be revoked before expiry. This is acceptable because the tokens are scoped to a single user/org and the threat model is low – a leaked refresh token grants the same access as a leaked API key. If revocation becomes necessary, a database-backed revocation list can be added later.

## Open Questions

[Section titled “Open Questions”](#open-questions)

1. **OAuth query param preservation across login redirect**: When an unauthenticated user hits `/ui/oauth/authorize`, the cookie auth middleware redirects to Zitadel login. After login, the user needs to land back at `/ui/oauth/authorize` with the original OAuth query params intact. Need to verify that the existing Zitadel redirect flow preserves the full original URL including query params.

# Multi-org CLI auth and default org config

> The CLI holds a single API key bound to one org, so users in several orgs cannot switch orgs without rewriting its config, and nothing ties a directory to an org.

Issues: <https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/issues/1940>, <https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/issues/2065>, <https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/issues/2129>

## Problem

[Section titled “Problem”](#problem)

The CLI holds exactly one credential. `internal/configfile` reads and writes `os.UserConfigDir()/gritz/config.json` (`~/.config/gritz/config.json` on Linux), whose only field is `File.Token`. API keys are bound to a single org server-side (`CreateKey` stamps `model.Key.OrgID` from the caller; bearer-key requests authenticate as that org), so the CLI is logged in to one org at a time:

* A user in several orgs has to rewrite `config.json`, or juggle env vars, to switch orgs.

* Nothing ties a repo or directory to an org, so a command run in the wrong checkout quietly acts on whichever org the configured key belongs to.

* No command writes the file. `gritz task`, `gritz logs` and `gritz shell` fail with “not authenticated, run setup first”, but there is no `setup` command.

* Each command gets its credential differently:

  | Command                                    | Credential source today                                                               |
  | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `task list/create/update`, `logs`, `shell` | `configfile.Load(nil)` → `config.json`                                                |
  | `mcp`, `notify`                            | `--token` / `GRITZ_TOKEN`, required; no config fallback; `--server` has no env source |
  | `runner`                                   | `--key` / `GRITZ_API_KEY`, falling back to `config.json`                              |

## Design

[Section titled “Design”](#design)

### Overview

[Section titled “Overview”](#overview)

* One file format, `.gritz.yml`, used at every level. It names orgs, holds their keys and servers, and selects one with `org`.
* Every user-facing command merges the `.gritz.yml` files from the working directory up to `/`, on top of `$CONFIG_DIR/.gritz.yml`, then selects one org entry. The entry supplies the server, org id and key.
* `--key` / `GRITZ_API_KEY` bypasses all of that, for CI and deployed runners.
* One new command, `gritz login`, writes an entry into `$CONFIG_DIR/.gritz.yml`. Everything else is done by editing the files by hand.

### The `.gritz.yml` format

[Section titled “The .gritz.yml format”](#the-gritzyml-format)

YAML, parsed with the `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` dependency that `workspaces.yaml` already uses. Every field is optional:

```yaml
org: acme
server: https://gritz.example.com
allowed: [acme, local]
orgs:
  acme:
    id: 12
    key: gritz_k_...
  local:
    id: 1
    server: http://localhost:8080
    key: gritz_k_...
```

* `orgs` maps a local name to an entry:

  * `id`: the org id (`orgs.id`).
  * `key`: an API key for that org, the `CreateKeyResponse.raw_token` string.
  * `server`: the server URL; omitted means the default server, `https://gritz.dev`. `login` always writes it.

* `org` names the entry used when none is selected explicitly. It matches the `--org` flag.

* `server` (top-level) is the server `gritz login` uses when `--server` isn’t given. It has no effect when entries are read.

* `allowed` lists the entry names that may be selected. Unset allows every entry.

Unknown fields are a parse error, so a typo like `ogr:` doesn’t silently do nothing.

**Names are local aliases.** The server only ever sees the key, which determines the org. Names exist so files and flags stay readable (`--org acme` instead of `--org 12`) and so one user can hold two keys for the same org (`acme`, `acme-ci`) or the same org id on two servers (`acme`, `local`). The id is kept in the entry so the file says which org a key is for, so `login` can recognise an existing entry, and so commands can build web UI links (`?org=12`). Because names never reach the server, there’s no need for a unique server-side slug.

Keys are read as is: there is no file-permission check. `login` creates `$CONFIG_DIR/.gritz.yml` with mode `0600`.

### Discovery and merge

[Section titled “Discovery and merge”](#discovery-and-merge)

Starting at the working directory, walk up one directory at a time to `/`, collecting every `<dir>/.gritz.yml` that exists. The walk does not stop at a git root. `$CONFIG_DIR/.gritz.yml` is always merged as the base layer, beneath everything the walk found. `$CONFIG_DIR` is `configfile.Dir()`, unchanged: `GRITZ_CONFIG_DIR`, else `os.UserConfigDir()/gritz`. A `.gritz.yml` path that exists but isn’t a regular file is an error.

Layers merge from the base up, so nearer files win:

* `org`, `allowed` and the top-level `server` each come from the nearest file that sets them.
* `orgs` merges by name. A nearer entry replaces a farther one with the same name whole; fields are not merged across files, so an id from one file can’t be paired with a key from another.

The merged result remembers which file set `org`, `allowed` and each entry, for error messages.

The intended layering:

* `$CONFIG_DIR/.gritz.yml` holds the user’s entries and keys, written by `login`.
* A `.gritz.yml` checked into a repo sets `org`, and optionally `allowed`, using names the team agrees on, and optionally the top-level `server` its org lives on. It holds no keys.
* A `.gritz.yml` in an uncommitted parent directory (`~/work/acme/.gritz.yml`) can pin everything below it, including several repos.

Nothing stops a committed `.gritz.yml` from holding `orgs` with keys; that’s the same risk as committing any other file containing a secret.

### Selection

[Section titled “Selection”](#selection)

Every user-facing command selects one entry at startup:

1. If `--key` / `GRITZ_API_KEY` is set, use that key, and skip the files, entries and `allowed` entirely (see Explicit key below).

2. Load and merge the files, and validate the result. An entry without `id` or `key` is an error naming the file it came from, and so is an `org` that isn’t in the merged `allowed`, whether or not either is the entry being selected:

   ```plaintext
   error: org "acme" (from /home/me/src/labs/.gritz.yml) is not in allowed [labs] (from /home/me/src/labs/.gritz.yml)
   ```

3. The selected name is `--org` / `GRITZ_ORG` if set, else the merged `org`. With neither:

   ```plaintext
   error: no org selected: pass --org or set org in a .gritz.yml file
   ```

4. If `allowed` is set and doesn’t contain the name, fail, naming the file that set `allowed`:

   ```plaintext
   error: org "local" is not allowed here: allowed is [acme] (from /home/me/src/acme/.gritz.yml)
   ```

5. If no merged entry has the name, fail, pointing at `login`:

   ```plaintext
   error: no org entry named "acme": run `gritz login --key <key> --name acme`
   ```

6. The entry supplies the org id, the key and the server.

**Server URL.** The selected entry’s `server` > `gritzclient.DefaultURL`. `--server` / `GRITZ_SERVER` never overrides an entry’s `server`: every entry `gritz login` writes carries its own, and an override could send the entry’s key to a server the user typed or inherited from the environment. `--server` without `--key` fails with `--server requires --key: entries in .gritz.yml carry their own server`. Either the files decide entry, key and server, or explicit credentials do. Every user-facing command gets the `GRITZ_SERVER` env source; `mcp` and `notify` lack it today. `Resolve` always sets `Server`, to `configfile.DefaultServer` (the same URL as `gritzclient.DefaultURL`) when nothing else does, so commands pass `BaseURL: cfg.Server` as is.

**Explicit key.** `--key` / `GRITZ_API_KEY` supplies a raw key directly. The key determines the org server-side, and the server is `--server` > `GRITZ_SERVER` > `gritzclient.DefaultURL`. `--org` / `GRITZ_ORG` and every `.gritz.yml` file are ignored. This is the path for CI and for runners deployed with an injected key.

### API change: report the caller’s org

[Section titled “API change: report the caller’s org”](#api-change-report-the-callers-org)

`login` has to learn which org a key belongs to. Nothing returns that today: `GetProfileResponse.default_org_id` is the user’s web-UI default, not the org the request authenticated as, and `GetProfile` reads the caller’s user, which an API key doesn’t have. Add a dedicated RPC:

```proto
rpc GetCaller(GetCallerRequest) returns (GetCallerResponse);


message GetCallerRequest {}


message GetCallerResponse {
  Org org = 1; // the org the request is authenticated against
}
```

`apiserver.GetCaller` loads the org from `apiauth.MustCaller(ctx).OrgID` with no user lookup, so it works for API keys, web UI sessions and MCP OAuth tokens alike. `GetProfile` is unchanged.

### CLI commands

[Section titled “CLI commands”](#cli-commands)

**`gritz login --key <key> [--name <name>] [--server <url>]`**

1. Call `GetCaller` with the key against `--server` (else `GRITZ_SERVER`, else the top-level `server` of the nearest `.gritz.yml` that sets one, walking up from the working directory to the base layer, else `configfile.DefaultServer`). A failure means the key is invalid; report it and write nothing.

2. The org id and name are `resp.org.id` and `resp.org.name`.

3. The entry name is `--name`, else a slug of the org name: lowercase, apostrophes dropped, each run of other non-alphanumeric characters becomes a single `-`, and leading and trailing `-` are trimmed (`Acme Labs` → `acme-labs`, `Ilia Choly's Org` → `ilia-cholys-org`). An empty slug is an error asking for `--name`.

4. Load `$CONFIG_DIR/.gritz.yml` alone, not the merged view. If it has an entry with that name:

   * for the same id and server, replace its key;
   * for a different id or server, fail: `entry "acme" is org 31 on https://gritz.dev; pass --name to add org 12 under another name`. An omitted `server` in a hand-written entry compares as `https://gritz.dev`.

5. Otherwise add `{id, key, server}` under the name. `server` is always written, including `https://gritz.dev`, so the entry doesn’t depend on which `.gritz.yml` files are around when it’s read.

6. If the file has no `org`, set it to the entry’s name, so the first org added is selected. An existing `org` is never changed.

7. Write the file to a temp file in `$CONFIG_DIR` and rename it into place, keeping its mode, or creating it `0600` if it didn’t exist. The file is re-marshalled, so comments and key order in it are not preserved.

8. Print `Logged in to Acme Labs (org 12) as "acme-labs"`.

The key is taken from `--key` only; there is no stdin or TTY prompt. `--key` here reads the same `GRITZ_API_KEY` env source as every other command, so `GRITZ_API_KEY=... gritz login` also works. Apart from step 6, `login` never touches `org`, and it never touches `allowed`.

There’s no `logout` and no `org` subcommand. Removing an entry, switching the selected `org` or restricting `allowed` is an edit to a `.gritz.yml` file.

**Existing commands**

Each user-facing command gets the same three flags, defined once by `configfile.Flags()` and appended to each command’s `Flags`:

| Flag             | Env             | Notes                                                   |
| ---------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--org`          | `GRITZ_ORG`     | new; an entry name                                      |
| `--key`, `-k`    | `GRITZ_API_KEY` | replaces `mcp`/`notify` `--token`/`GRITZ_TOKEN`         |
| `--server`, `-s` | `GRITZ_SERVER`  | requires `--key`; plus the env source on `mcp`/`notify` |

Each command’s action replaces its `configfile.Load` + `cfg.Token == ""` block (or `cmd.String("token")`) with one `configfile.Resolve(cmd)` call, which runs the selection above and returns the entry to use. The command builds its client options inline from it, `gritzclient.Options{BaseURL: e.Server, Token: e.Key, ...}`, and the same way for `NotificationClientOptions` and `shell.Attach`:

* `task list`, `task create`, `task update`, `logs`, `shell`: drop the `configfile.Load(nil)` blocks. `shell` also passes the selected key to `shell.Attach` in place of `cfg.Token`.
* `mcp`: `--token` (required) is replaced by selection. A Claude Code MCP config of `{"command": "gritz", "args": ["mcp"]}` launched from a repo picks up the repo’s `org` without a token in the config. The notification client gets the same key and server.
* `notify`: same change as `mcp`. Running one `notify` per org with `--org` is how to watch several orgs.
* `runner`: `configfile.Load(&Overrides{Token: ...})` is replaced by the same selection, so a runner on a laptop uses an entry from `.gritz.yml`. Deployed runners keep using `GRITZ_API_KEY`.

**Not changed:** `gritz tool agent-mcp`, the GitHub MCP proxy and the git credential helper run inside the sandbox with the task JWT on `--token`/`GRITZ_TOKEN`. They never read `.gritz.yml`, and they keep their flags. `server`, `driver`, `containers`, `workspaces`, `download` and `version` don’t authenticate as a user.

### Dropped state

[Section titled “Dropped state”](#dropped-state)

Per the no-backwards-compatibility policy there’s no import path:

* `$CONFIG_DIR/config.json` (`configfile.File{Token}`) is no longer read, and its code is deleted. Users run `gritz login` once per org.
* `--token` / `GRITZ_TOKEN` on `gritz mcp` and `gritz notify` are removed. MCP configs that pass `--token` need the flag dropped, or switched to `--key` / `GRITZ_API_KEY`.
* The “run setup first” error messages go away with the `configfile.Load` call sites.

`workspaces.yaml` and `prebuilt/` stay in `$CONFIG_DIR`, and `configfile.Dir()` doesn’t change. The old `config.json` isn’t deleted automatically; it’s just ignored.

### API

[Section titled “API”](#api)

```go
package configfile // github.com/gritzapp/gritz/internal/configfile


// Dir returns the gritz config directory: GRITZ_CONFIG_DIR, else os.UserConfigDir()/gritz.
func Dir() (string, error) // unchanged


// Name is the file name used at every level.
const Name = ".gritz.yml" // new


// Entry is one named org in a .gritz.yml file.
type Entry struct { // new
  // ID is the org id.
  ID int64 `yaml:"id"`
  // Key is an API key for the org.
  Key string `yaml:"key"`
  // Server is the server URL; empty means the default server.
  Server string `yaml:"server,omitempty"`
}


// File is the contents of one .gritz.yml file.
type File struct { // replaced: was {Token}
  // Org is the entry name selected when none is given.
  Org string `yaml:"org,omitempty"`
  // Server is the server `gritz login` uses when --server isn't given. It
  // has no effect on reading entries.
  Server string `yaml:"server,omitempty"`
  // Allowed lists the entry names that may be selected; nil allows all.
  Allowed []string `yaml:"allowed,omitempty"`
  // Orgs maps local names to entries.
  Orgs map[string]Entry `yaml:"orgs,omitempty"`
}


// Read parses the .gritz.yml file at path, rejecting unknown fields.
func Read(path string) (*File, error) // new


// Merged is the result of merging .gritz.yml files, nearest winning.
type Merged struct { // new
  Org         string
  OrgFrom     string // path of the file that set Org
  Server      string // the nearest top-level server, used only by `gritz login`
  Allowed     []string
  AllowedFrom string // path of the file that set Allowed
  Orgs        map[string]Entry
  OrgsFrom    map[string]string // entry name -> path of the file that set it
}


// LoadOptions configures Load.
type LoadOptions struct { // new
  Dir  string // where the walk starts
  Root string // the last directory the walk visits; empty means /
  Base string // the base layer; empty means $CONFIG_DIR/.gritz.yml
}


// Load merges the base layer and every .gritz.yml from opts.Dir up to opts.Root.
func Load(opts LoadOptions) (*Merged, error) // replaced: was Load(*Overrides) (*File, error)


// Login writes entry under name into the .gritz.yml file at path, replacing the
// key of an existing entry with the same id and server, and failing with
// ErrNameTaken if name belongs to a different org or server. It sets org to
// name when the file has none. The caller validates the key and sets
// entry.Server.
func Login(path, name string, entry Entry) error // new


// LoginServer returns the server `gritz login` uses when --server isn't
// given: the top-level server of the nearest .gritz.yml from the working
// directory, else DefaultServer.
func LoginServer() (string, error) // new


// ErrNameTaken is returned by Login when name is in use by another org or server.
var ErrNameTaken = errors.New("entry name in use") // new


// Validate checks that the entry has an id and a key.
func (e Entry) Validate() error // new


// IsAllowed reports whether org may be selected: Allowed is unset or lists it.
func (m *Merged) IsAllowed(org string) bool // new


// Validate checks that Org is allowed and that every entry is complete,
// returning errors that name the file responsible.
func (m *Merged) Validate() error // new


// Lookup returns the entry named org, or m.Org when org is empty,
// enforcing m.Allowed. Call Validate first.
func (m *Merged) Lookup(org string) (*Entry, error) // new


// Flags returns the --org, --key and --server flags (GRITZ_ORG, GRITZ_API_KEY,
// GRITZ_SERVER) shared by user-facing commands. --server requires --key.
func Flags() []cli.Flag // new


// DefaultServer is the server URL used when nothing sets one; it matches
// gritzclient.DefaultURL.
const DefaultServer = "https://gritz.dev" // new


// Resolve applies --key, --server and --org from cmd and the merged .gritz.yml
// files from the working directory, and returns the entry to use. With --key,
// the entry has only Key and Server, and Server is --server, else
// DefaultServer. --server requires --key. Without --key, Server is the
// entry's server, else DefaultServer.
func Resolve(cmd *cli.Command) (*Entry, error) // new


// Slug turns an org name into an entry name, returning "" if nothing is left.
func Slug(orgName string) string // new


type Overrides struct{ ... }       // removed
func Path() (string, error)        // removed
func Save(f *File) error           // removed
```

```go
package command // github.com/gritzapp/gritz/internal/command


var LoginCommand *cli.Command // new: gritz login
```

**How it fits:** `configfile` owns everything about how a command finds its credentials: the file format, discovery, merging, selection, the shared flags, and the `login` write. `Merged.Validate` and `Merged.Lookup` hold the selection rules and take no urfave/cli types, so they can be table-tested against a `Merged` value. `Resolve` is the only part that reads the command: it takes `--key` as is, or calls `Load` with the working directory, `Validate`, and `Lookup` with `--org`, then applies the server precedence and returns the `Entry`. `configfile` doesn’t build client options and doesn’t reference `gritzclient` at all, and there’s no helper in `gritzclient` either. Every user-facing command appends `configfile.Flags()...`, calls `configfile.Resolve` in its action, and builds `gritzclient.Options` (and `NotificationClientOptions` or the `shell.Attach` arguments) inline from the entry’s `Server` and `Key`. `LoginCommand` calls `configfile.LoginServer` when `--server` isn’t given, then `GetCaller`, `configfile.Slug` and `configfile.Login`.

## Implementation Plan

[Section titled “Implementation Plan”](#implementation-plan)

1. **Report the caller’s org** — Delivers: the `GetCaller` RPC (proto, regenerated code, `apiserver.GetCaller`). Depends on: nothing. Verifiable by: an e2e API test where `GetCaller` with a key in a non-default org returns that org.
2. **`.gritz.yml` load, merge and select** — Delivers: `configfile.Entry`, the new `File` shape under a temporary name beside the old one, `Read`, `Load` under a temporary name, `Entry.Validate`, `Merged.IsAllowed`, `Merged.Validate` and `Merged.Lookup`, and `Slug`. Nothing calls them yet. Depends on: nothing. Verifiable by: unit tests over temp dirs: the walk merges past a `.git` directory up to the temp root; the base layer is always merged; `org`/`allowed` come from the nearest file; entries replace whole by name; an `org` outside `allowed`, a disallowed `--org` and a missing entry each fail naming the right file (table tests on `Validate` and `Lookup` over `Merged` values); unknown fields fail.
3. **`gritz login`** — Delivers: `configfile.Login`, `LoginCommand` and `main.go` registration. Depends on: (1), (2). Verifiable by: unit tests for `Slug` and for `Login` (new entry, key replaced for same id and server, `ErrNameTaken` otherwise, `org` set only when absent); an e2e test that creates a key, runs `gritz login --key`, and checks the written entry.
4. **Wire existing commands and delete the old config** — Delivers: `configfile.Flags`/`configfile.Resolve`; `task`, `logs`, `shell`, `mcp`, `notify` and `runner` switched over; `mcp`/`notify` `--token` removed; the old `File`/`Load`/`Save`/`Overrides`/`Path` and `config.json` handling deleted and the step-2 names taken over; docs updated (`reference/cli`, `using/cli`, `integrations/mcp`, `operators/runner`). Depends on: (2), (3). Verifiable by: an e2e test that logs in to two orgs and runs `gritz task list` from a directory whose `.gritz.yml` sets `org` to org A while the base layer selects org B, and sees only org A’s tasks; and one where `--org` names an entry outside `allowed` and fails.

## Trade-offs

[Section titled “Trade-offs”](#trade-offs)

* **One format at every level vs. a global config plus a repo file.** Separate files let the repo file be locked down to `org:` only, but they need two parsers, two sets of rules and a key store on the side. One format with one merge rule is simpler to explain and lets any directory, not just a repo, carry a full configuration. The cost is that nothing structurally prevents a key in a committed file.
* **Walk to `/` vs. stop at the git root.** Stopping at `.git` scopes a file to its repo, but it rules out a parent directory pinning several checkouts (`~/work/acme/.gritz.yml`). Because files merge rather than the nearest one winning outright, a stray parent `.gritz.yml` can only supply defaults that nearer files override, and `allowed` lets a repo refuse entries it doesn’t expect.
* **Whole-entry vs. field-wise merge of `orgs`.** Field-wise merging would let a committed file declare `acme: {id: 12}` and a private one add the key, but it would also let a key from one file be used under an id or server from another. Whole-entry replacement keeps each entry self-consistent.
* **Local names vs. org ids.** Server-side org names aren’t unique and can be renamed, and adding a unique slug column is a schema change with its own UX. Local names sidestep both: the user chooses them, they never reach the server, and `login` derives a sensible default.
* **Keys in the config file vs. a separate key store or OS keychain.** A keychain is more secure at rest but adds a cgo or D-Bus dependency and fails in headless and container environments. Keeping the key in the entry means one file holds everything about an org, which is what makes hand-editing the whole workflow. No permission check is enforced; `login` creates the file `0600`.
* **YAML vs. JSON vs. TOML.** YAML is already a dependency, used for `workspaces.yaml`, and allows comments in a committed `.gritz.yml`. JSON doesn’t allow comments, and TOML would add a dependency.
* **One `login` command vs. a full `logout`/`org` command set.** Commands to list, remove and switch entries would each be a thin wrapper over an edit to a short YAML file. Leaving them out keeps the CLI surface to one command, and `login` exists only because it’s the step that needs the server.
