```protobuf
// RuleCondition constrains one attribute of an event. Comparisons are exact and
// case-sensitive.
message RuleCondition {
  string attr = 1;
  string op = 2;  // One of "equals", "prefix" or "contains".
  string value = 3;
}


message RoutingRule {
  reserved 3, 4, 6, 7, 8;  // Previously: prefix, mention, assignee, url_prefix, value (legacy flat matchers)
  string source = 1;
  string type = 2;
  CreateTaskAction create = 5;
  // Whether a match starts the subscribed tasks again to handle the event.
  // When false, the event is added to their timelines without starting them.
  // Rules created in the web UI default to true.
  bool wakeup = 9;
  // Conditions the event must meet, all of them. Empty source and type match
  // any; no conditions match every event of the selected type.
  repeated RuleCondition conditions = 10;
  // Whether the rule also acts on events from people who aren't members of the
  // org. False (the default) acts only on members' events.
  bool public = 11;
  // The rule's namespace: a match looks for subscribed tasks only in it, and a
  // task the rule creates is in it. Empty is the default namespace.
  string namespace = 12;
}


message CreateTaskAction {
  string workspace = 1;
  string runner = 2;
  string prompt = 3;
  // The auto-archive delay of the tasks the rule creates, as in
  // Task.auto_archive.
  google.protobuf.Duration auto_archive = 4;
}


message GetRoutingRulesRequest {}


message GetRoutingRulesResponse {
  repeated RoutingRule rules = 1;
}


message SetRoutingRulesRequest {
  repeated RoutingRule rules = 1;
}


message SetRoutingRulesResponse {
  repeated RoutingRule rules = 1;
}


// AttrDef is an event attribute a routing rule can have a condition on.
message AttrDef {
  string key = 1;  // The name a RuleCondition's attr refers to.
  string label = 2;        // The attribute's name in the routing-rule editor.
  string help = 3;         // Help text for the attribute in the routing-rule editor.
  string placeholder = 4;  // Placeholder for the attribute's value in the routing-rule editor.
}


// It mirrors the eventrouter registry entry, exposing only the client-relevant
// fields (the shipped default rules are intentionally omitted).


// EventTypeDef is an event type, identified by its source and type, and every
// attribute a routing rule can have a condition on for it.
message EventTypeDef {
  string source = 1;
  string type = 2;
  string label = 3;
  repeated AttrDef attrs = 4;
}


message GetEventTypesRequest {}


message GetEventTypesResponse {
  repeated EventTypeDef event_types = 1;
}


message GetCustomEventTypesRequest {}


message GetCustomEventTypesResponse {
  repeated EventTypeDef event_types = 1; // every source is "custom"
}


// SetCustomEventTypesRequest replaces the org's custom event types. It fails
// with `invalid_argument` if a type is malformed, and `failed_precondition` if
// an existing routing rule would no longer be valid with the new types.
message SetCustomEventTypesRequest {
  repeated EventTypeDef event_types = 1;
}


message SetCustomEventTypesResponse {
  repeated EventTypeDef event_types = 1;
}


// TestEventRequest composes an event and routes it through the org's routing
// rules, as a dry run or for real. Every event is validated against its type:
// it fails with `invalid_argument` for an unknown source or type, a missing or
// non-absolute http(s) url, or an attr the type doesn't declare. An event of a
// built-in source routes as the caller. A custom event routes like one posted
// to the custom event webhook: it has no actor, so only public rules match it.
message TestEventRequest {
  string source = 1;                // The event type's source, such as "github".
  string type = 2;                  // The event type, such as "issue_comment".
  // The event's attribute values, keyed by AttrDef.key. An attr may have
  // several values. "body" and "url" are sent in their own fields, not here.
  map<string, AttrValues> attrs = 3;
  string description = 4;           // Optional description shown on the task's timeline; defaults to the event type's label.
  bool fire = 5;                    // False (the default) for a dry run; true to act on the matches.
  map<string, string> details = 6;  // Stored as the event's ExternalPayload.details.
  string body = 7;                  // The event's text, matched by rules on the "body" attr.
  string url = 8;                   // The event's resource URL, matched by rules on the "url" attr and by subscribed links.
}


// AttrValues is the values of one event attribute.
message AttrValues {
  repeated string values = 1;
}


message TestEventResponse {
  repeated TestEventMatch matches = 1;  // The match in the caller's org, if any.
  bool fired = 2;                       // Whether the matches were acted on.
}


// TestEventMatch is what a matching routing rule did, or would do.
message TestEventMatch {
  int64 org_id = 1;
  int32 rule_index = 2;      // The index of the rule that matched, or -1 for a built-in default rule.
  bool would_wake = 3;       // The matched rule's wakeup.
  bool would_create = 5;     // Whether a task would be, or was, created.
  repeated int64 created_task_ids = 6;   // The tasks created; set only when fired.
  repeated int64 event_ids = 7;          // The events added; set only when fired.
}


message CreateGitHubTokenRequest {}


message CreateGitHubTokenResponse {
  string token = 1;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp expires_at = 2;
}


// See docs/src/content/docs/proposals/implemented/scheduled-tasks.md.


// Schedule is a task template and a cron expression: the server creates a task
// from the template at each time the expression matches. A schedule belongs to
// its org, not to the user who created it.
message Schedule {
  int64 id = 1;
  string name = 2;
  string workspace = 3;
  string runner = 4;
  string namespace = 5;
  repeated Instruction instructions = 6;
  string cron_expr = 7;
  string timezone = 8;                      // IANA name; default "UTC".
  bool enabled = 9;
  google.protobuf.Duration auto_archive = 10;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp next_run_at = 11;  // Unset when disabled.
  google.protobuf.Timestamp last_run_at = 12;  // Unset when it has never run.
  int64 last_task_id = 13;                  // 0 when it has never run.
  string created_by = 14;                   // Who created it; grants no permissions.
  google.protobuf.Timestamp created_at = 15;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp updated_at = 16;
}


message CreateScheduleRequest {
  string name = 1;
  string workspace = 2;
  string runner = 3;
  string namespace = 4;
  repeated Instruction instructions = 5;
  string cron_expr = 6;
  string timezone = 7;                      // IANA name; empty defaults to "UTC".
  // Whether the schedule runs. False (the default) creates a schedule that
  // never runs until SetScheduleEnabled enables it.
  bool enabled = 8;
  google.protobuf.Duration auto_archive = 9;
}


message CreateScheduleResponse {
  Schedule schedule = 1;
}


message GetScheduleRequest {
  int64 id = 1;
}


message GetScheduleResponse {
  Schedule schedule = 1;
}


message ListSchedulesRequest {}


message ListSchedulesResponse {
  repeated Schedule schedules = 1;
}


// UpdateScheduleRequest replaces a schedule's template, cron expression and
// timezone. Changing cron_expr or timezone recomputes next_run_at. Use
// SetScheduleEnabled to enable or disable it.
message UpdateScheduleRequest {
  int64 id = 1;
  string name = 2;
  string workspace = 3;
  string runner = 4;
  string namespace = 5;
  repeated Instruction instructions = 6;
  string cron_expr = 7;
  string timezone = 8;                      // IANA name; empty defaults to "UTC".
  google.protobuf.Duration auto_archive = 9;
}


message UpdateScheduleResponse {
  Schedule schedule = 1;
}


message DeleteScheduleRequest {
  int64 id = 1;
}


message DeleteScheduleResponse {}


// SetScheduleEnabledRequest enables or disables a schedule. Enabling computes
// next_run_at from now; disabling clears it, and the schedule stops running.
message SetScheduleEnabledRequest {
  int64 id = 1;
  bool enabled = 2;
}


message SetScheduleEnabledResponse {
  Schedule schedule = 1;
}


// RunScheduleRequest creates a task from a schedule now, once, in addition to
// its regular runs. It leaves next_run_at, last_run_at and last_task_id
// unchanged, and works on a disabled schedule too, so a schedule can be tried
// out before it is enabled.
message RunScheduleRequest {
  int64 id = 1;
}


message RunScheduleResponse {
  Task task = 1;  // The task the run created.
}
```

# CLI

> Every gritz subcommand and flag, with its environment variable and default.

The `gritz` binary holds the CLI, the server, the runner and the tools that run inside sandboxes. This page lists every subcommand and flag; [Using the CLI](/pr/2141/using/cli/) shows how to use the everyday ones.

```plaintext
gritz [--help] [--version] <command> [flags] [args]
```

`--help` (`-h`) works on every command, and `--version` (`-v`) prints the version, as `gritz version` does. Where a flag has an environment variable, the flag wins when both are set.

## Authentication

[Section titled “Authentication”](#authentication)

`gritz task`, `gritz logs`, `gritz shell`, `gritz mcp`, `gritz notify` and `gritz runner` take these flags, which pick the organisation, API key and server:

| Flag             | Environment     |                                                                                         |
| ---------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--org`          | `GRITZ_ORG`     | The organisation’s name in the `.gritz.yml` files. Defaults to their `org`.             |
| `--key`, `-k`    | `GRITZ_API_KEY` | An API key to use instead of the `.gritz.yml` files and `--org`.                        |
| `--server`, `-s` | `GRITZ_SERVER`  | The server URL to use with `--key`, which it requires. Defaults to `https://gritz.dev`. |

Without `--key`, a command merges `.gritz.yml` in the config directory with every `.gritz.yml` from the working directory up to `/`, the nearest winning, and uses the organisation it selects, on that organisation’s `server`, otherwise `https://gritz.dev`. See [Configuration](/pr/2141/using/cli/#configuration).

The config directory is `GRITZ_CONFIG_DIR` if set, otherwise `gritz` under the user config directory (`~/.config/gritz` on Linux).

### `gritz login`

[Section titled “gritz login”](#gritz-login)

Asks the server which organisation an API key belongs to, and saves the key under a name in `.gritz.yml` in the config directory. Logging in again with a new key for the same organisation and server replaces the key. The server is always saved with the organisation. If the file has no `org`, the name becomes it.

| Flag             | Environment     | Default                                                                                         |                            |
| ---------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `--key`, `-k`    | `GRITZ_API_KEY` |                                                                                                 | The API key. Required.     |
| `--name`         |                 | the organisation’s name, in lowercase with dashes                                               | The name to save it under. |
| `--server`, `-s` | `GRITZ_SERVER`  | the top-level `server` of the nearest `.gritz.yml` that sets one, otherwise `https://gritz.dev` | The server URL.            |

## Tasks

[Section titled “Tasks”](#tasks)

### `gritz task create`

[Section titled “gritz task create”](#gritz-task-create)

Creates a task and starts it, then prints it as JSON. It also takes the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

| Flag                  | Environment | Default   |                                                                                                                                                          |
| --------------------- | ----------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--runner`, `-r`      |             |           | The runner to run on. Required.                                                                                                                          |
| `--workspace`, `-w`   |             | `default` | The workspace.                                                                                                                                           |
| `--instruction`, `-i` |             |           | An instruction. Repeat it for several.                                                                                                                   |
| `--name`, `-n`        |             |           | The task’s name.                                                                                                                                         |
| `--auto-archive`      |             | `0`       | The [auto-archive](/pr/2141/concepts/tasks/#auto-archive) delay, such as `24h`. `0` is never; a negative value archives the task as soon as it finishes. |

### `gritz task list`

[Section titled “gritz task list”](#gritz-task-list)

Prints the organisation’s 50 newest unarchived tasks as JSON. It takes only the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

### `gritz task update <task-id>`

[Section titled “gritz task update \<task-id>”](#gritz-task-update-task-id)

Changes a task. It needs at least one of `--add-instruction`, `--start`, `--name` or `--auto-archive`. It also takes the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

| Flag                      | Environment | Default |                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------- | ----------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--add-instruction`, `-i` |             |         | Add an instruction. Repeat it for several.                                                                                                      |
| `--start`, `-r`           |             |         | Start the task. A running task isn’t interrupted: it runs again when its current run ends.                                                      |
| `--name`, `-n`            |             |         | Rename the task.                                                                                                                                |
| `--auto-archive`          |             |         | Set the auto-archive delay. `0` is never; a negative value archives the task as soon as it finishes. Left out, the task keeps the delay it has. |

### `gritz logs <task-id>`

[Section titled “gritz logs \<task-id>”](#gritz-logs-task-id)

Prints a task’s log. It also takes the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

| Flag             | Environment | Default |                                             |
| ---------------- | ----------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `--follow`, `-f` |             |         | Keep printing new output.                   |
| `--interval`     |             | `2s`    | How often `--follow` checks for new output. |

### `gritz shell <task-id>`

[Section titled “gritz shell \<task-id>”](#gritz-shell-task-id)

Opens an interactive shell in a task’s sandbox, relayed through the server. See [A shell in the sandbox](/pr/2141/operators/debugging/#a-shell-in-the-sandbox). It takes only the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

## Clients

[Section titled “Clients”](#clients)

### `gritz mcp`

[Section titled “gritz mcp”](#gritz-mcp)

Runs a local MCP server over stdio, for Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP clients. See [MCP](/pr/2141/integrations/mcp/#connect-with-gritz-mcp). It also takes the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

| Flag             | Environment | Default |                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------- | ----------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--auto-archive` |             |         | The auto-archive delay for tasks created without an `auto_archive` argument.                                                                                                       |
| `--channel`      |             | off     | Push task updates into the Claude Code session as [channel](/pr/2141/integrations/mcp/#channels) messages, and add the `channel_mute`, `channel_unmute` and `channel_muted` tools. |

### `gritz notify`

[Section titled “gritz notify”](#gritz-notify)

Shows a desktop notification each time one of the organisation’s tasks completes, fails or is cancelled, until stopped. It also takes the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

| Flag      | Environment | Default |                           |
| --------- | ----------- | ------- | ------------------------- |
| `--title` |             | `gritz` | The notifications’ title. |

### `gritz runner`

[Section titled “gritz runner”](#gritz-runner)

Runs a runner. Its flags are described in [Runner](/pr/2141/operators/runner/#flags). It also takes the [authentication](#authentication) flags.

| Flag                      | Environment                   | Default                                   |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `--workspaces`, `-w`      |                               | `workspaces.yaml` in the config directory |
| `--id`                    | `GRITZ_RUNNER_ID`             | the hostname                              |
| `--backend`               | `GRITZ_BACKEND`               | `docker`                                  |
| `--concurrency`           |                               | `5`                                       |
| `--state-db`              | `GRITZ_STATE_DB`              | `/var/lib/gritz/runner.db`                |
| `--poll`                  |                               | `30s`                                     |
| `--lambda-microvm-region` | `GRITZ_LAMBDA_MICROVM_REGION` | the AWS SDK’s region                      |
| `--local-root`            | `GRITZ_LOCAL_ROOT`            |                                           |
| `--debug`                 |                               | off                                       |

`--backend` also accepts `local`, which runs agents directly on the runner’s host, without isolation, in sandboxes under `--local-root`. It is for tests and development.

### `gritz download`

[Section titled “gritz download”](#gritz-download)

Downloads the prebuilt driver binaries a runner needs from the latest GitHub release. See [Driver binaries](/pr/2141/operators/runner/#driver-binaries).

| Flag            | Default          |                                                   |
| --------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `--github-repo` | `gritzapp/gritz` | The repository to download from, as `owner/repo`. |

### `gritz workspaces`

[Section titled “gritz workspaces”](#gritz-workspaces)

Loads a workspace config, with its `${env:}` and `${sh:}` expansions, and prints the result, to check it before restarting a runner.

| Flag             | Default           |                                                      |
| ---------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `--config`, `-c` | `workspaces.yaml` | The file to load, relative to the current directory. |

### `gritz containers`

[Section titled “gritz containers”](#gritz-containers)

Lists the gritz containers on this host’s Docker, running or not.

| Flag      |                                               |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `--prune` | Remove every stopped gritz container instead. |

### `gritz version`

[Section titled “gritz version”](#gritz-version)

Prints the version.

## Inside the sandbox

[Section titled “Inside the sandbox”](#inside-the-sandbox)

These commands run inside a task’s sandbox. The runner and the workspace config start them; you don’t run them yourself.

### `gritz driver`

[Section titled “gritz driver”](#gritz-driver)

The driver server, which the runner’s backend starts in each sandbox. It runs the setup commands and the agent, and ships the task’s log.

| Flag                    | Default |                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--addr`                | `:8080` | The TCP address or `unix:///path` to serve on.                                                                      |
| `--prefix`              | `/`     | A directory prepended to every path the driver uses in the sandbox.                                                 |
| `--aws-lambda-hooks`    | off     | Also answer the Lambda MicroVM lifecycle hooks.                                                                     |
| `--aws-lambda-validate` |         | An executable to run on the Lambda MicroVM image’s validate hook, to warm the snapshot. Needs `--aws-lambda-hooks`. |

### `gritz tool agent-mcp`

[Section titled “gritz tool agent-mcp”](#gritz-tool-agent-mcp)

The MCP server behind the [agent tools](/pr/2141/using/agent-tools/). The runner adds it to every agent’s MCP config.

| Flag                |                                                                                                      |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--task`, `-t`      | The task ID. Required.                                                                               |
| `--runner`, `-r`    | The runner ID. Required.                                                                             |
| `--workspace`, `-w` | The workspace. Required.                                                                             |
| `--token`           | The task’s token. Required.                                                                          |
| `--server`, `-s`    | The server URL. Defaults to `https://gritz.dev`.                                                     |
| `--capability`      | A [capability](/pr/2141/operators/workspaces-yaml/#capabilities) of the task. Repeat it for several. |

### `gritz tool github-mcp`

[Section titled “gritz tool github-mcp”](#gritz-tool-github-mcp)

An MCP server over stdio that forwards to GitHub’s MCP server with GitHub App installation tokens, rotating them before they expire. For workspaces with the `github_token` capability; see [GitHub credentials for agents](/pr/2141/integrations/github/#github-credentials-for-agents).

| Flag        | Environment    | Default                              |                                                                     |
| ----------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--server`  | `GRITZ_SERVER` | `https://gritz.dev`                  | The server URL.                                                     |
| `--token`   | `GRITZ_TOKEN`  |                                      | The task’s token.                                                   |
| `--url`     |                | `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/` | GitHub’s MCP endpoint.                                              |
| `--min-ttl` |                | `5m`                                 | Rotate to a new token when the current one has less than this left. |

### Hidden commands

[Section titled “Hidden commands”](#hidden-commands)

`gritz --help` doesn’t list these two:

* `gritz tool git-credential`: a git credential helper that answers with GitHub App installation tokens, for workspaces with the `github_token` capability. It takes `--server` (`GRITZ_SERVER`) and `--token` (`GRITZ_TOKEN`). Configure it with `git config --global credential.https://github.com.helper "!gritz tool git-credential"`.
* `gritz tool proxy --addr <addr>`: connects its stdin and stdout to a TCP address or `unix:///path`. The Docker backend uses it to reach the driver’s socket.

# Custom event envelope

> The request and response of POST /webhook/custom, with every field, its validation, authentication and status codes.

The custom events webhook accepts one event per request. The [custom events guide](/pr/2141/integrations/custom-events/) shows how to set it up; this page is the precise contract.

## Request

[Section titled “Request”](#request)

```plaintext
POST /webhook/custom
Authorization: Bearer xat_…
Content-Type: application/json
```

The full URL is on **Settings → Organisation**, in the **Custom Events** card; for gritz.dev it is `https://gritz.dev/webhook/custom`. The webhook only handles `POST`.

### Authentication

[Section titled “Authentication”](#authentication)

* The request must carry `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A request without it gets `401 bearer token required`, even from a browser with a signed-in session: the webhook doesn’t accept session cookies.
* The token is an API key (`xat_…`) from the **Keys** page. A wrong, deleted or expired key gets `401 invalid or expired token`.
* The token must hold the `event:create` scope, or the request gets `403 permission denied`. API keys hold every scope. A task’s own token does not hold `event:create`.
* The event belongs to the key’s organisation and is checked against that organisation’s custom event types. It has no actor, so only the organisation’s public routing rules can match it.

### Body

[Section titled “Body”](#body)

A JSON object of at most 1 MiB:

```json
{
  "type": "alert",
  "description": "checkout-api error rate alert",
  "url": "https://alerts.example.com/alerts/4211",
  "body": "checkout-api error rate above 5% for 10 minutes",
  "attrs": {"severity": ["critical"], "service": ["checkout-api"]},
  "details": {"runbook": "https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/checkout-api"}
}
```

Fields other than the six below are rejected, as are fields of the wrong JSON type.

| Field         | Type                                | Required | Validation                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `type`        | string                              | yes      | Must name one of the organisation’s custom event types, as defined on **Events → Custom Schemas**. A type named like a built-in GitHub or Jira type still only resolves to the custom one. |
| `description` | string                              | no       | The event’s description on the task’s timeline. Defaults to the type’s label.                                                                                                              |
| `url`         | string                              | yes      | Must be non-empty and an absolute `http` or `https` URL with a host. Only GitHub and Jira URLs are normalised: see [`url`](#url).                                                          |
| `body`        | string                              | no       | The event’s text. Defaults to the empty string.                                                                                                                                            |
| `attrs`       | object of string → array of strings | no       | Every key must be an attribute the type declares, other than `body` and `url`.                                                                                                             |
| `details`     | object of string → string           | no       | Not validated.                                                                                                                                                                             |

#### `type`

[Section titled “type”](#type)

The custom type’s name, which matches `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$`. The type’s label becomes the event’s description on the task’s timeline when `description` is empty.

#### `url`

[Section titled “url”](#url)

The resource the event is about, and the key that routes it: an event wakes the tasks subscribed to its `url`, and a task created by the event is subscribed to it.

gritz normalises GitHub and Jira issue URLs to one key per issue, as it does for their native events, so a custom event about a GitHub pull request or a Jira issue wakes the task subscribed to it:

| `url`                                                                                                                       | Key                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pull/{n}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment            | `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pull/{n}` |
| `https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pulls/{n}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment | `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}` or `/pull/{n}` |
| `https://{site}.atlassian.net/browse/{KEY}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment                              | `https://{site}.atlassian.net/browse/{KEY}`                   |
| `https://{site}.atlassian.net/rest/api/{version}/issue/{KEY}`, with any further path segments, query or fragment            | `https://{site}.atlassian.net/browse/{KEY}`                   |

The host must match exactly (`github.com`, not `www.github.com`), and the key always uses `https`. A Jira REST URL with a numeric issue id instead of a key, and a GitHub API comment URL (`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/comments/{id}`), are not normalised.

Every other URL is used exactly as sent, so events about the same resource must send the same URL byte for byte.

#### `body`

[Section titled “body”](#body-1)

The event’s text, passed to the agent. Rules match on it through the `body` attribute every custom type declares.

#### `attrs`

[Section titled “attrs”](#attrs)

The values routing rule conditions match on, keyed by attribute. Each value is a list of strings; a condition matches when any value in the list satisfies it. An attribute the type declares may be omitted, in which case conditions on it don’t match. Sending `body` or `url` here is an error: send them as the top-level fields, from which their attributes are derived.

#### `details`

[Section titled “details”](#details)

Free-form key/value strings stored with the event and shown with it to the agent and in the Web UI. Rules can’t match on them.

## Response

[Section titled “Response”](#response)

A valid event gets `200 OK` with a JSON body:

```json
{"routed": 1}
```

`routed` is the number of tasks the event was delivered to: tasks created by the matching rule, or existing tasks subscribed to the event’s `url`. It is `0` when no public rule for the type matches, or when a rule matches but no task is subscribed to the `url` and the rule doesn’t create tasks.

Errors are plain text.

## Status codes

[Section titled “Status codes”](#status-codes)

| Status | Body                                                | Cause                                                                                                                               |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `200`  | `{"routed": n}`                                     | The event was valid and routed to `n` tasks, possibly none.                                                                         |
| `400`  | `invalid envelope: …`                               | The body is not a JSON object matching the envelope: invalid JSON, an unknown field, a field of the wrong type, or more than 1 MiB. |
| `400`  | `unknown event type "…"`                            | `type` is empty or not one of the organisation’s custom types.                                                                      |
| `400`  | `url is required`                                   | `url` is missing or empty.                                                                                                          |
| `400`  | `url "…" must be an absolute http or https URL`     | `url` is relative, has no host, or has another scheme.                                                                              |
| `400`  | `attr "…" must be sent as the envelope's "…" field` | `attrs` has a `body` or `url` key.                                                                                                  |
| `400`  | `attr "…" not declared by event type "…"`           | `attrs` has a key the type doesn’t declare.                                                                                         |
| `401`  | `bearer token required`                             | No `Authorization: Bearer` header.                                                                                                  |
| `401`  | `invalid or expired token`                          | The bearer token is not a valid, unexpired API key or gritz token.                                                                  |
| `403`  | `permission denied`                                 | The token lacks the `event:create` scope.                                                                                           |
| `500`  | `internal error`                                    | The server failed to load the custom types or to route the event.                                                                   |

# Event types

> Every built-in GitHub and Jira event type, with its source and type, its label in the Web UI, and the attributes routing rule conditions can match.

Every event has a source and a type, such as `github` and `issue_comment`. A [routing rule](/pr/2141/concepts/routing-rules/) matches one `(source, type)` pair, which the rule form’s **Event type** list shows by its label, such as **GitHub: Issue/PR Comment**. Its conditions then test the event’s attributes.

This page lists the built-in types, from the [GitHub](/pr/2141/integrations/github/) and [Jira](/pr/2141/integrations/jira/) integrations. An organisation’s own types have the source `custom` and the attributes their schema defines; see [Custom events](/pr/2141/integrations/custom-events/).

## Attributes

[Section titled “Attributes”](#attributes)

Every type has two attributes:

* `body`: the event’s text. For a comment or a review it is that text; for the other types it is the description of the issue or pull request.
* `url`: the event’s own URL. For a comment or a review it is the comment’s or review’s URL; for the other types it is the issue’s or pull request’s URL.

Each type adds others. An attribute can hold several values, such as every user mentioned in a comment, and a condition holds if any of them satisfies it. Conditions compare exactly and are case-sensitive; see [Matching](/pr/2141/concepts/routing-rules/#matching).

The **Label** column is what the rule form shows for the attribute.

## GitHub

[Section titled “GitHub”](#github)

Source `github`. GitHub usernames are given without the leading `@`.

### `issue_comment`

[Section titled “issue_comment”](#issue_comment)

**GitHub: Issue/PR Comment.** A comment on an issue or a pull request is created or edited.

| Attribute | Label        | Value                                                                                   |
| --------- | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Comment Body | The comment’s text.                                                                     |
| `url`     | Comment URL  | The comment’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/123#issuecomment-456`. |
| `mention` | Mention      | Each username @-mentioned in the comment.                                               |
| `user`    | User         | The username of the commenter.                                                          |

### `pull_request_review_comment`

[Section titled “pull_request_review_comment”](#pull_request_review_comment)

**GitHub: PR Review Comment.** An inline review comment on a pull request is created or edited.

| Attribute | Label               | Value                                                                                       |
| --------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Review Comment Body | The review comment’s text.                                                                  |
| `url`     | Review Comment URL  | The review comment’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123#discussion_r456`. |
| `mention` | Mention             | Each username @-mentioned in the review comment.                                            |
| `user`    | User                | The username of the reviewer.                                                               |

The event also carries, for the agent but not for conditions, the file and line the comment is on (`path`, `line`, `start_line`, `side`) and its `diff_hunk`.

### `pull_request_review`

[Section titled “pull_request_review”](#pull_request_review)

**GitHub: PR Review.** A review with a summary is submitted on a pull request.

| Attribute | Label       | Value                                                                                     |
| --------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Review Body | The review’s summary.                                                                     |
| `url`     | Review URL  | The review’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123#pullrequestreview-456`. |
| `mention` | Mention     | Each username @-mentioned in the summary.                                                 |
| `user`    | User        | The username of the reviewer.                                                             |

### `issue_assigned`

[Section titled “issue_assigned”](#issue_assigned)

**GitHub: Issue Assigned.** An issue is assigned to someone.

| Attribute  | Label      | Value                                                                |
| ---------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`     | Issue Body | The issue’s description.                                             |
| `url`      | Issue URL  | The issue’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/123`. |
| `assignee` | Assignee   | The username newly assigned.                                         |
| `user`     | User       | The username of who assigned it.                                     |

### `pull_request_assigned`

[Section titled “pull_request_assigned”](#pull_request_assigned)

**GitHub: PR Assigned.** A pull request is assigned to someone.

| Attribute  | Label    | Value                                                                     |
| ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`     | PR Body  | The pull request’s description.                                           |
| `url`      | PR URL   | The pull request’s URL, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123`. |
| `assignee` | Assignee | The username newly assigned.                                              |
| `user`     | User     | The username of who assigned it.                                          |

### `pull_request_opened`

[Section titled “pull_request_opened”](#pull_request_opened)

**GitHub: PR Opened.** A pull request is opened.

| Attribute | Label          | Value                           |
| --------- | -------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `body`    | PR Description | The pull request’s description. |
| `url`     | PR URL         | The pull request’s URL.         |
| `user`    | User           | The username of who opened it.  |

### `pull_request_closed`

[Section titled “pull_request_closed”](#pull_request_closed)

**GitHub: PR Closed.** A pull request is closed, with or without merging.

| Attribute | Label            | Value                                          |
| --------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | PR Description   | The pull request’s description.                |
| `url`     | PR URL           | The pull request’s URL.                        |
| `state`   | Merged or Closed | `merged` if it was merged, otherwise `closed`. |
| `user`    | User             | The username of who closed or merged it.       |

### `label_added`

[Section titled “label_added”](#label_added)

**GitHub: Label Added.** A label is added to an issue or a pull request. Adding several labels sends one event per label.

| Attribute | Label         | Value                                      |
| --------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `body`    | Issue/PR Body | The issue’s or pull request’s description. |
| `url`     | Issue/PR URL  | The issue’s or pull request’s URL.         |
| `label`   | Label         | The label added.                           |
| `user`    | User          | The username of who added it.              |

## Jira

[Section titled “Jira”](#jira)

Source `atlassian`. People are identified by their Atlassian account ID, such as `5b10ac8d82e05b22cc7d4ef5`. Enter the bare ID, not the `[~accountid:…]` form Jira uses in comment text.

### `comment_created`

[Section titled “comment_created”](#comment_created)

**Jira: Issue Comment.** A comment is added to an issue.

| Attribute | Label        | Value                                                                                                  |
| --------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `body`    | Comment Body | The comment’s text.                                                                                    |
| `url`     | Comment URL  | The comment’s URL, such as `https://your-domain.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-123?focusedCommentId=10001`. |
| `mention` | Mention      | The account ID of each person @-mentioned in the comment.                                              |
| `user`    | User         | The account ID of the commenter.                                                                       |

### `label_added`

[Section titled “label_added”](#label_added-1)

**Jira: Label Added.** One or more labels are added to an issue. Adding several at once sends one event with all of them.

| Attribute | Label             | Value                                                                         |
| --------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `body`    | Issue Description | The issue’s description.                                                      |
| `url`     | Issue URL         | The issue’s URL, such as `https://your-domain.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-123`. |
| `label`   | Label             | Each label added.                                                             |
| `user`    | User              | The account ID of who added them.                                             |

### `issue_assigned`

[Section titled “issue_assigned”](#issue_assigned-1)

**Jira: Issue Assigned.** An issue is assigned to someone.

| Attribute  | Label             | Value                               |
| ---------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `body`     | Issue Description | The issue’s description.            |
| `url`      | Issue URL         | The issue’s URL.                    |
| `assignee` | Assignee          | The account ID of the new assignee. |
| `user`     | User              | The account ID of who assigned it.  |

## URLs and subscriptions

[Section titled “URLs and subscriptions”](#urls-and-subscriptions)

The `url` attribute is the event’s own URL, as listed above, so a `url` condition sees the comment’s or review’s URL, with its fragment or query string. Use `prefix` to scope a rule to a repository or a project: `url prefix https://github.com/owner/repo/` or `url prefix https://your-domain.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-`.

To find subscribed tasks, gritz reduces the URL to the issue or pull request it belongs to, so an event about a comment reaches the tasks subscribed to its issue. See [Subscriptions](/pr/2141/concepts/events-and-links/#subscriptions).

# Agent tools

> The gritz tools every agent gets (get_my_task, update_my_task, create_link, report and get_github_token), what gritz tells agents to do with them, and how to write instructions that use them.

gritz adds an MCP server named `gritz` to every agent it runs, alongside the MCP servers in the task’s [workspace](/pr/2141/concepts/workspaces/). Its tools let the agent read and update its own task, and nothing else: they work with a token that only grants access to that task (see [Task tokens](/pr/2141/concepts/orgs-members-keys/#task-tokens)).

## What agents are told

[Section titled “What agents are told”](#what-agents-are-told)

On a task’s first run, before your instructions, gritz tells the agent to:

* name the task with `update_my_task` if it has no name;
* create a link with `subscribe=true` for each resource it creates, such as a pull request, an issue or a comment, so replies reach the task even after it finishes, and `subscribe=false` for reference links it didn’t create;
* prefer URLs a person can open over API URLs;
* use `report` for anything you should see, since its text replies aren’t shown;
* answer questions or problems on the platform the latest instruction or event came from, such as the pull request, and say which task it is from;
* call `get_my_task` if it needs to check for updates mid-run.

Then it gives the agent the task: its instructions, events and links, so it doesn’t need a tool call to start. On later runs the agent gets only what is new. See [Instructions and runs](/pr/2141/concepts/tasks/#instructions-and-runs).

## Tools

[Section titled “Tools”](#tools)

### `get_my_task`

[Section titled “get_my_task”](#get_my_task)

Returns the task: its ID, name, status, workspace, [namespace](/pr/2141/concepts/namespaces/) and URL, its links, and its instructions and events in order. Reports and status changes aren’t included.

### `update_my_task`

[Section titled “update_my_task”](#update_my_task)

Renames the task. It takes `name`, the new name. Agents can’t change anything else about their task, including its auto-archive delay.

### `create_link`

[Section titled “create_link”](#create_link)

Links the task to an external resource, and appears on the task’s timeline and in its sidebar.

| Parameter   |                                                                           |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `url`       | The resource’s URL.                                                       |
| `relevance` | How the resource relates to the task, such as “PR implementing the fix”.  |
| `title`     | Optional. A title to show for the link.                                   |
| `subscribe` | Optional. `true` to have events about the resource delivered to the task. |

A subscribed link is how a task hears about review comments on its pull request, or replies on its Jira issue. Which events wake it is up to the organisation’s [routing rules](/pr/2141/concepts/routing-rules/). See [Events and links](/pr/2141/concepts/events-and-links/).

### `report`

[Section titled “report”](#report)

Posts `message` to the task’s timeline. This is how an agent tells you what it did, what it found or what is blocking it: the agent’s own replies only appear in the task’s log.

### `get_github_token`

[Section titled “get_github_token”](#get_github_token)

Meant to return a short-lived GitHub token for the organisation’s GitHub App installation. Only tasks whose workspace has the `github_token` [capability](/pr/2141/operators/workspaces-yaml/#capabilities) get this tool, and the server doesn’t issue these tokens yet, so the tool always fails.

Agents get GitHub access today from their workspace instead: a token under `secrets:`, such as `GH_TOKEN`, which `gh`, git and the GitHub MCP server can use. See [`secrets`](/pr/2141/operators/secrets/).

## Writing instructions that use them

[Section titled “Writing instructions that use them”](#writing-instructions-that-use-them)

The agent already uses these tools as above without being asked. Mention them when you want something specific:

* **To get a summary where you’ll see it**: “When you’re done, report a summary of the changes and anything you couldn’t do.”
* **To keep a task listening**: “Open a draft pull request and link it with subscribe=true.” The task finishes, and a review comment on the pull request wakes it if a routing rule matches.
* **To link context you gave it**: “Link the incident page as a reference, not subscribed.”
* **To name it predictably**: “Name this task `deps: bump <package>`.”

The agent’s other tools, such as for GitHub or Jira, come from the MCP servers and credentials in its workspace. Ask your operator what a workspace provides, or see [`workspaces.yaml`](/pr/2141/operators/workspaces-yaml/).

# CLI

> Use the gritz CLI to create, list and update tasks, read a task's log, open a shell in its sandbox and get desktop notifications, and log in to one or more organisations.

The `gritz` binary is the CLI as well as the runner and server. Release binaries for Linux are attached to each [GitHub release](https://github.com/gritzapp/gritz/releases); to build it from a checkout, run `mise run install`.

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

The CLI authenticates with an [API key](/pr/2141/concepts/orgs-members-keys/#api-keys), and acts in the organisation the key belongs to. Create one on the **Keys** page and log in with it:

```bash
gritz login --key xat_...
```

```plaintext
Logged in to Acme Labs (org 12) as "acme-labs"
```

`gritz login` asks the server which organisation the key belongs to and saves the key under a name in `.gritz.yml` in the gritz config directory. The name is the organisation’s name in lowercase with dashes, unless `--name` gives another, and the first organisation you log in to becomes the selected `org`. Log in once for each organisation you work in:

```yaml
org: acme-labs
orgs:
  acme-labs:
    id: 12
    key: xat_...
    server: https://gritz.dev
  personal:
    id: 3
    key: xat_...
    server: https://gritz.dev
```

The config directory is `GRITZ_CONFIG_DIR` if set, otherwise `gritz` under your user config directory: `~/.config/gritz` on Linux, `~/Library/Application Support/gritz` on macOS.

### Choosing an organisation

[Section titled “Choosing an organisation”](#choosing-an-organisation)

Every command acts in one organisation: the one `--org` (or `GRITZ_ORG`) names, otherwise the `org` of the `.gritz.yml` files.

```bash
gritz task list --org personal
```

A `.gritz.yml` file can also live in any directory, such as a repository or a folder of checkouts. A command reads every `.gritz.yml` from the directory it runs in up to `/`, on top of the one in the config directory, and the nearest file wins. Organisations of the same name replace each other whole. A repository can pick its organisation without holding a key:

```yaml
org: acme-labs
allowed: [acme-labs]
```

`allowed` lists the organisations that can be used below the file; a command run there with any other `--org` fails, and so does every command if the `org` isn’t allowed. Every field is optional, and an unknown field is an error.

### Server

[Section titled “Server”](#server)

Every command talks to the organisation’s `server`, or to `https://gritz.dev` if it has none. `gritz login` saves the server you give it with `--server` (`-s`) or the `GRITZ_SERVER` environment variable:

```bash
gritz login --key xat_... --server https://gritz.example.com
```

Without `--server`, it uses the top-level `server` of the nearest `.gritz.yml` that sets one, otherwise `https://gritz.dev`, so a repository can name the server its organisation lives on:

```yaml
server: https://gritz.example.com
```

The top-level `server` is read only by `gritz login`.

### Key without a config file

[Section titled “Key without a config file”](#key-without-a-config-file)

`--key` (`-k`) or the `GRITZ_API_KEY` environment variable gives a command its key directly, for CI and other places with no config file. The command then reads no `.gritz.yml` files and ignores `--org`, and talks to `--server`, `GRITZ_SERVER` or `https://gritz.dev`. Other than in `gritz login`, `--server` and `GRITZ_SERVER` need a key this way, since an organisation in a `.gritz.yml` carries its own server:

```bash
GRITZ_API_KEY=xat_... gritz task list
```

## Tasks

[Section titled “Tasks”](#tasks)

### `gritz task create`

[Section titled “gritz task create”](#gritz-task-create)

Creates a task and starts it straight away, then prints it as JSON.

```bash
gritz task create -r my-runner -w pets-workshop \
  -i "Add a --json flag to the list command and open a pull request."
```

| Flag                  |                                                                                                                                                                                |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `--runner`, `-r`      | The [runner](/pr/2141/concepts/runners/) to run on. Required.                                                                                                                  |
| `--workspace`, `-w`   | The [workspace](/pr/2141/concepts/workspaces/). Defaults to `default`.                                                                                                         |
| `--instruction`, `-i` | An instruction. Repeat it for several.                                                                                                                                         |
| `--name`, `-n`        | The task’s name. The agent names it if you don’t.                                                                                                                              |
| `--auto-archive`      | The [auto-archive](/pr/2141/concepts/tasks/#auto-archive) delay, such as `1h` or `24h`. `0`, the default, is never; a negative value archives the task as soon as it finishes. |

The **Workspaces** page in the Web UI lists runner IDs and their workspaces.

### `gritz task list`

[Section titled “gritz task list”](#gritz-task-list)

Prints the organisation’s 50 newest unarchived tasks as JSON, with their status, runner, workspace and URL.

### `gritz task update`

[Section titled “gritz task update”](#gritz-task-update)

Changes a task.

```bash
gritz task update 1234 --start -i "Also update the README."
```

| Flag                      |                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--add-instruction`, `-i` | Add an instruction. Repeat it for several.                                                                                                  |
| `--start`, `-r`           | Start the task, as the Web UI does when you send an instruction. A running task isn’t interrupted: it runs again when its current run ends. |
| `--name`, `-n`            | Rename the task.                                                                                                                            |
| `--auto-archive`          | Set the auto-archive delay. Left out, the task keeps the delay it has.                                                                      |

An instruction added without `--start` waits on the task until something else starts it, such as an event or a later `--start`.

Cancelling, restarting and archiving tasks are done in the [Web UI](/pr/2141/using/web-ui/#the-task-page).

## `gritz logs`

[Section titled “gritz logs”](#gritz-logs)

Prints a task’s log: the setup commands, the agent’s output and gritz’s own lines, as the Web UI’s **Logs** view shows them. It works for any task in the organisation, including tasks whose sandbox is gone.

```bash
gritz logs 1234     # print the log so far
gritz logs -f 1234  # and keep following it
```

`--interval` sets how often `-f` checks for new output, `2s` by default.

## `gritz shell`

[Section titled “gritz shell”](#gritz-shell)

Opens an interactive shell in a finished task’s sandbox, to look at what the agent left behind:

```bash
gritz shell 1234
```

The runner starts the sandbox again with a shell in place of the agent. It works whatever the runner’s backend and wherever it runs: the server relays the session, so you need no access to the runner. See [A shell in the sandbox](/pr/2141/operators/debugging/#a-shell-in-the-sandbox).

## `gritz notify`

[Section titled “gritz notify”](#gritz-notify)

Stays running and shows a desktop notification each time one of the organisation’s tasks completes, fails or is cancelled.

```bash
gritz notify
```

Run one `gritz notify --org <name>` for each organisation to watch several.

`--title` sets the notifications’ title, `gritz` by default. It uses `notify-send` on Linux and the system notifications on macOS and Windows.

## Other commands

[Section titled “Other commands”](#other-commands)

* `gritz mcp` runs a local MCP server that lets Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP clients create and manage tasks; see [MCP](/pr/2141/integrations/mcp/).
* `gritz runner`, `gritz download`, `gritz workspaces` and `gritz containers` are for running a runner; see [Runner](/pr/2141/operators/runner/) and [Debugging](/pr/2141/operators/debugging/).
* `gritz version` prints the CLI’s version.

[CLI reference](/pr/2141/reference/cli/) lists every command and flag.

# Web UI

> A tour of the gritz Web UI, the task list and task page, schedules, events and routing rules, workspaces, members, keys and settings.

The Web UI is served by the gritz server under `/ui/`, for example `https://gritz.dev/ui/`. It updates live: task statuses, timelines and logs change as they happen, without reloading. The dot next to the organisation selector shows whether the live connection is up.

The bar at the top links to every page, and holds the organisation selector, the light and dark theme toggle, **Settings** and **Logout**. Press Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac) anywhere to jump to a task by name.

## Tasks

[Section titled “Tasks”](#tasks)

**Tasks** lists the organisation’s tasks, newest first, with their runner, workspace and [status](/pr/2141/concepts/tasks/#statuses). A `command:` badge next to the status is an action the runner hasn’t carried out yet. Turn on **Show archived** to include archived tasks, and archive or unarchive a task from its row.

**+ Task** creates a task. Pick a runner, then one of its workspaces; the name, [namespace](/pr/2141/concepts/namespaces/) and [auto-archive](/pr/2141/concepts/tasks/#auto-archive) delay are optional. The form remembers the last runner and workspace you used. The task is created as a draft, and starts when you send its first instruction.

## The task page

[Section titled “The task page”](#the-task-page)

The sidebar on the left holds the task’s status and name, its three views, its details (runner, workspace, namespace, created and updated times), its links, and its actions:

* **Archive** or **Unarchive**. When an auto-archive delay is counting down, the time left shows next to it.
* **Cancel**, while the task is pending or running.
* **Restart**, once it is running or finished.
* **Auto-archive**, to change the delay: never, immediately, 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours or 7 days.

The arrow at the top collapses the sidebar to icons.

### Timeline

[Section titled “Timeline”](#timeline)

The timeline is everything that happened to the task, in order: your instructions, events from GitHub, Jira and custom sources, the agent’s reports, links it created, and status changes with who caused them. It opens at the latest entry and loads older ones as you scroll up.

The box at the bottom sends an instruction: Enter sends it, Shift+Enter adds a new line. A finished task starts again with it; a running task picks it up when its current run ends. See [Instructions and runs](/pr/2141/concepts/tasks/#instructions-and-runs).

### Logs

[Section titled “Logs”](#logs)

The task’s log, as the sandbox writes it: setup commands, the agent’s messages and tool calls, and gritz’s own lines. It follows new output while the task runs. Declared [secrets](/pr/2141/operators/secrets/) are masked.

### Shell

[Section titled “Shell”](#shell)

A terminal in the task’s sandbox, for looking at what the agent left behind. It can be opened once the task has finished, and works like [`gritz shell`](/pr/2141/using/cli/#gritz-shell): the runner starts the sandbox again with a shell in place of the agent.

## Schedules

[Section titled “Schedules”](#schedules)

**Schedules** lists the organisation’s [schedules](/pr/2141/concepts/schedules/) with their cron expression, timezone, next run and workspace, and the task each created last. From each row you can turn a schedule on or off, run it now, edit it or delete it. **+ Schedule** creates one.

## Events

[Section titled “Events”](#events)

**Events** has three tabs:

* **Routing Rules**: the organisation’s [routing rules](/pr/2141/concepts/routing-rules/), in the order they are checked, with their event type, conditions and action. Reorder them with the arrows, edit or remove them, add one with **+ Rule**, or try an event against them with **Test**.
* **Recent Events**: the latest events delivered to the organisation’s tasks. Open one to see its description, URL, data and the task it reached.
* **Custom Schemas**: the organisation’s custom event types. See [Custom events](/pr/2141/integrations/custom-events/).

## Workspaces

[Section titled “Workspaces”](#workspaces)

**Workspaces** lists the [workspaces](/pr/2141/concepts/workspaces/) the organisation’s [runners](/pr/2141/concepts/runners/) have registered, with their description, runner and when they were last registered. Filter by runner, and **Clear** to remove the listed runner’s workspaces, or every runner’s.

## Members and Keys

[Section titled “Members and Keys”](#members-and-keys)

**Members** lists the organisation’s members and their role. The owner adds members by email here and removes them. **Keys** lists the organisation’s API keys and creates and deletes them. See [Organisations, members and API keys](/pr/2141/concepts/orgs-members-keys/).

## Settings

[Section titled “Settings”](#settings)

**Settings** has two tabs:

* **Account**: the organisations you own, where you create new ones and delete them, and your linked [Atlassian](/pr/2141/integrations/jira/#link-your-atlassian-account) and [GitHub](/pr/2141/integrations/github/#link-your-github-account) accounts. Linking them lets [routing rules](/pr/2141/concepts/routing-rules/#public-rules) recognise your comments as a member’s.
* **Organisation**: the URLs and settings that connect the organisation to other systems: the [MCP server URL](/pr/2141/integrations/mcp/) for MCP clients, the [custom events](/pr/2141/integrations/custom-events/) webhook URL, the [GitHub App installation](/pr/2141/integrations/github/#install-the-github-app), and the [Atlassian webhook](/pr/2141/integrations/jira/#connect-jira) URL and secret.

The server’s version is at the bottom of the page.
